items.title: Fani-Kayode refused interview after live-stream ‘exclusion’ — SABC
items.description: The South African Broadcasting Corporation, SABC, has said Nigeria’s High Commissioner to the country, Femi Fani-Kayode, declined an interview invitation, following his protest over the exclusion of his speech from a livestream of a diplomatic ceremony hosted by President Cyril Ramaphosa. Read Also: South Africa releases Fani-Kayode’s speech after protest The SABC, in a statement issued yesterday, said it regretted the envoy’s decision but remained open to engaging with him and the Nigerian High Commission. The response followed Fani-Kayode’s complaint that his introduction and speech were omitted from the broadcaster’s livestream of the presentation of letters of credence ceremony held at the Sefako Makgatho Presidential Guest House in Pretoria on Friday. “We regret that the High Commissioner declined an interview with SABC News, reportedly because of his dissatisfaction with the livestream of the ceremony. We respect his decision and remain open to engaging with him and the Nigerian High Commission,” the statement said. Notably, the SABC did not address the specific allegation that Fani-Kayode’s presentation was excluded from the livestream of the ceremony. It, however, rejected the description of it as a state broadcaster, insisting that it was a public service media organisation committed to independent, impartial and credible journalism. “Two points need clarifying. First, the SABC is a public service media, not a state broadcaster. Our mandate is to serve the public interest through independent, impartial and credible journalism. The Presidency’s livestream arrangements and SABC News’ editorial coverage are separate matters. “Secondly, SABC News did cover the ceremony. It was carried on the SABC News LIVE channel on SABC+, and the High Commissioner’s arrival was shown during a live crossing on the SABC News Channel (DStv Channel 404). We also published a clip on our official X account of the High Commissioner speaking to President Cyril Ramaphosa. “The SABC remains committed to upholding the principles of fairness, impartiality and editorial independence in its coverage, as well as value our longstanding relationship with Nigeria,” the statement read. Recall that Fani-Kayode had earlier accused the South African Presidency of deliberately excluding Nigeria’s delegation from the livestream of the ceremony, which involved 15 ambassadors presenting their letters of credence to Ramaphosa. The envoy said the introductions and speeches of 14 other ambassadors were broadcast, while Nigeria’s segment was omitted, with the livestream resuming after he had concluded his address. He also disclosed that he declined an interview offered by SABC News at the venue, saying he had been displeased with the treatment of the Nigerian delegation. However, the South African Presidency later released the full video of the ceremony, including Fani-Kayode’s speech, on its YouTube channel. The controversy subsequently sparked a public exchange between the Nigerian High Commission and Vincent Magwenya, spokesperson for Ramaphosa. The post Fani-Kayode refused interview after live-stream ‘exclusion’ — SABC appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Assemblies to face sanctions over illegal billboards – Deputy Minister
items.description: The Deputy Minister for Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, Rita Naa Odoley Sowah, has warned Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives (MMDCEs) that they will be held responsible for unauthorised billboards and advertising structures erected within their jurisdictions. She said the various assemblies must take ownership of enforcement efforts and ensure that advertisers comply with regulations governing the installation of outdoor advertising structures. Madam Sowah issued the warning during a joint billboard inspection and enforcement exercise organised by the Ministry, in collaboration with the Advertising Association of Ghana (AAG), in Accra on Sunday, November 15, 2026. She stressed that no individual or advertising company may erect a billboard or advertising sign without first securing approval from the relevant assembly. “As the MMDCEs have spoken, we are looking forward to them taking charge of their various jurisdictions from today onwards. As we have started, we want them to take full charge so that, wherever they see any illegal billboards or advertising signs, they will take the necessary action,” she stated. The Deputy Minister also cautioned landowners against independently granting permission to advertisers to mount structures on their properties, explaining that the relevant assemblies have the authority to issue permits. The exercise follows a deadline issued to billboard owners and advertising companies to display their names and company details prominently on their structures to facilitate identification and regulatory enforcement. Inspection teams visited selected roads and areas in Accra with high concentrations of billboards, identified structures that breach applicable standards and regulatory requirements, and removed them through established procedures. Madam Sowah urged operators with unauthorised structures to dismantle them voluntarily to avoid enforcement action and additional financial penalties. “If you do not do that, the assemblies are going to surcharge you, and you pay something to them for pulling down your billboards,” she warned.

items.title: India, England, Australia and New Zealand to host all ICC events from 2028-31
items.description: LAHORE: Pakistan failed to get any event of the International Cricket Council (ICC) at least till 2031, as the game’s world governing body announced its activity programme for the 2028-2035 cycle on Sunday. According to a press release issued by the ICC, India, England, Australia and New Zealand swept all the events to be held from 2028 to 2031. From 2032 to 2035, the venues of the rema­ining events will be decided later. India, having a major influence in the ICC’s affairs, will host the 2029 ICC Champions Trophy and the 2031 ICC World Cup jointly with Bangladesh. Australia and New Zealand will organise the 2028 T20 World Cup. England will continue to host the ICC Test Championship final in 2029 and 2030, while it will also hold the 2030 T20 World Cup along with Ireland and Scotland. Surprisingly, Pakistan, an important stakeholder of the cricketing world which successfully hosted the eight-team Champions Trophy last year, was not given any ICC event. “The decisions were made with increasing opportunities for Full and Associate Members in mind, strengthening qualification pathways and enhancing competitive standards across international cricket,” the ICC said in a press release. Commenting on the announcement of the activity programme, Sanjog Gupta, the ICC chief executive, said: “The ICC events portfolio and schedule are critical components of cricket’s global architecture and deliver elevated context, competitiveness and consequence to the ecosystem. These tournaments serve as pinnacle moments for fans and players alike, with the associated pathways driving aspiration and access for the broader cricketing landscape.” MARQUEE MEN’S EVENTS SCHEDULE The ICC Board approved the windows for established ICC marquee men’s events until 2035. The confirmed schedule runs from the 2028 Men’s T20 World Cup in Australia and New Zealand up to the 2035 Men’s World Cup. The 2027 Men’s World Cup Qual­ifier, scheduled for February-March, will feature 10 teams and 23 matches. The tournament will comprise two groups of five, followed by semi-finals and a final, with the top four teams qualifying for the World Cup. The winners will progress directly to the 2027 Men’s World Cup Group Stage, while the three remaining teams will compete in the Super Series to determine the final Group Stage spot. The 16-team Global Qualifier, scheduled to be played during the first quarter of 2028, will feature 31 matches, with four groups of four competing across the group stage, quarter-finals, semi-finals and the final. A total of eight teams will qualify directly to the 2028 Men’s T20 World Cup from the event. The highest-placed team from each region will qualify, subject to minimum performance criteria, with the remaining places going to the next highest-placed teams overall. 2028 WOMEN’S T20 WORLD CUP QUALIFIER With the qualification framework for the 2028 Women’s T20 World Cup approved in May 2026, regional allocations for the Global Qualifier have now been confirmed. The Netherlands and Scotland, having participated in the 2026 tournament without securing automatic qualification for 2028, will be joined at the Global Qualifier by eight teams from regional qualifying. Those eight teams will advance through five regional qualification events scheduled for 2027, with two spots each up for grabs across Africa, Asia and the East Asia-Pacific, and one more from both the Americas and Europe. The top two teams from the Global Qualifier will secure the final places at the ICC Women’s T20 World Cup 2028. Host nations and dates have been confirmed for the final qualification events for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. The men’s qualifier for LA28 will take place from Feb 5-13, 2028 in Bangladesh, prior to the ICC Women’s Qualifier, which will run from Feb 26 to March 5, 2028 in the United States. The events constitute the final stage of the qualification pathway for cricket’s return to the Olympic programme at LA28. They will each feature eight teams — spread across two groups of four — and 13 matches. Each team will play the other teams in their group once, with the group winners progressing to the final. The winners of the final will secure the final qualification berth for the LA28 Olympic Games. Published in Dawn, November 16th, 2026

items.title: Medias publics : l’AIB ouvre son bureau régional de l’Ouest
items.description: Le ministre de la Communication, de la Culture, des Arts et du Tourisme, Pingdwendé Gilbert Ouédraogo, a lancé, le vendredi 13 novembre 2026 à Bobo-Dioulasso, les activités du bureau régional de l’Ouest de l’Agence d’information du Burkina (AIB). L’installation de l’AIB à Bobo-Dioulasso vise à rapprocher l’agence des populations et à assurer une meilleure couverture de l’actualité dans l’Ouest du Burkina Faso. L’Agence d’information du Burkina Faso (AIB) a installé un bureau régional à Bobo-Dioulasso. Cette antenne régionale de Bobo-Dioulasso couvre l’Ouest du pays. Le ministre de la Communication, de la Culture, des Arts et du Tourisme, Porte-parole du gouvernement, Pingdwendé Gilbert Ouédraogo, a procédé, le vendredi 13 novembre 2026, à l’ouverture officielle de ce bureau régional de l’AIB à Bobo-Dioulasso. A l’occasion, le directeur général de l’AIB, Enock Noufou Kindo, a laissé entendre que le bureau régional de Bobo-Dioulasso vise à renforcer la présence et les activités de l’AIB dans la région du Guiriko. Elle traduit selon lui, la volonté de l’agence de se rapprocher davantage des populations, des partenaires et de l’ensemble des acteurs. « Nous formulons le vœu que ce bureau régional soit un véritable espace de proximité, de collaboration, d’efficacité et de rayonnement au service de nos missions et du Burkina Faso », a affirmé le DG de l’AIB. Le ministre de la Communication, de la Culture, des Arts et du Tourisme, a ajouté que l’implantation de l’AIB à Bobo-Dioulasso a pour but de rapprocher davantage l’information des populations, de valoriser les réalités de nos territoires et de faire entendre la voix de toutes les composantes de notre Nation.« Aujourd’hui, en nous implantant à Bobo-Dioulasso, nous réaffirmons notre volonté de faire entendre la voix du grand Ouest, de donner une plus grande visibilité à ses réalités et de faire rayonner ses initiatives dans l’espace médiatique national et international. Il s’agit de faire en sorte que nos territoires ne soient plus de simples sujets de l’actualité, mais deviennent pleinement des espaces de production de l’information et de construction de notre récit national », a-t-il dit. Dans ce contexte sécuritaire, le ministre Gilbert Ouédraogo a souligné que le Burkina Faso a plus que besoin d’une information rigoureuse, vérifiée, responsable et profondément ancrée dans nos réalités. « Face aux rumeurs, aux infox et aux tentatives de manipulation de l’opinion, notre responsabilité est de contribuer, par le professionnalisme et la crédibilité de nos productions, à la préservation de la cohésion sociale et au renforcement de la confiance entre les citoyens », a martelé le ministre en charge de la communication. Il a souhaité que ce bureau régional soit un espace de vérité et de responsabilité, un vecteur de cohésion et de paix, un creuset de valorisation de nos initiatives locales et un instrument au service du développement de la région du Guiriko et de la nation tout entière. Pour permettre à l’AIB-Bobo de mener à bien sa mission, le ministre de la Communication, de la Culture, des Arts et du Tourisme, Pingdwendé Gilbert Ouédraogo a remis au directeur de l’AIB du matériel composé entre autres de dictaphones, d’appareils photo et d’ordinateurs. Adaman DRABO

items.title: KWSC completes maintenance work but water shortage persists in Karachi
items.description: KARACHI: Although the Karachi Water and Sewerage Corporation (KWSC) claimed to have restored water supply across the city after completing its annual maintenance work at the Dhabeji pumping station, many areas were still without water for a third consecutive day on Sunday. The utility had announced that the maintenance work that began on Nov 13 would cause a shortfall of around 130 million gallons per day (MGD) in water supply. On Sunday, it said in a statement that various technical and maintenance works, including the installation of valves at key locations and repairs to water pipelines, were completed during the annual maintenance operation. It added all 21 pumps at the Dhabeji pumping station were now operational and water supply across the city had been restored. It added that water supply to some affected areas, including Landhi, Korangi, Malir and Shah Faisal towns, was being gradually brought back to normal. However, the statement did not mention any time frame for when the supply would be normalised. According to a KWSC spokesperson, during the annual maintenance work, repairs to water pipelines were carried out at Dhabeji, Pipri, Shahrah-i-Bhutto and the Haleji conduits to improve, stabilise and enhance the efficiency of the water supply system. The spokesperson added that a new 60-inch-diameter valve had been installed at the Dhabeji pumping station during the maintenance work. Similarly, necessary repairs were carried out at all pump houses at the Pipri pumping station. While approximately 150-foot-long water pipeline along the alignment of Shahrah-i-Bhutto was replaced, a leakage in the Haleji conduit was also repaired. Published in Dawn, November 16th, 2026

items.title: Every family should have a Family Pharmacist: The future of personalised pharmaceutical care in Ghana
items.description: Healthcare is changing rapidly, and Ghana must keep exploring innovative approaches to improve its population’s health and well-being. One such approach is to introduce and promote Family Pharmacist services, so every family can access a designated pharmacist who understands their pharmaceutical and medication-related needs. I strongly advocate that every family in Ghana should have the opportunity to engage a Family Pharmacist who can provide continuous pharmaceutical care, medication counselling, health education, preventive health advice, and support for the safe and effective use of medicines. Pharmacists are among society’s most accessible healthcare professionals. However, the pharmacist’s role extends far beyond dispensing medicines. Modern pharmacy practice has evolved into a highly specialised clinical profession, with pharmacists contributing to patient care across a wide range of therapeutic and public health areas. Today, pharmacists have advanced expertise in oncology and chemotherapy, neuropharmacy, clinical pharmacy, infectious diseases, critical care, cardiology, paediatrics, geriatrics, psychiatry, public health, pharmacogenomics, antimicrobial stewardship, nuclear pharmacy, and several other specialised areas. These specialist pharmacists possess advanced knowledge and clinical skills that enable them to contribute meaningfully to the care of patients with complex diseases and medication needs. They work as part of multidisciplinary healthcare teams alongside physicians, nurses, and other healthcare professionals. Ghana should therefore consider a more structured model of pharmaceutical care in which the Family Pharmacist serves as a trusted pharmaceutical healthcare partner for the family, while patients with complex conditions can be referred to the appropriate specialist pharmacist. The Family Pharmacist could provide services including medication reviews, medication reconciliation, identification of potential drug interactions, support for medication adherence, counselling on the appropriate use of medicines, guidance on over-the-counter medications, health education, and advice on disease prevention. The Family Pharmacist could also maintain an appropriate medication record for family members and, where necessary, collaborate with doctors, nurses, hospitals, and specialist pharmacists to ensure continuity of care. For patients with complex medical conditions, the Family Pharmacist could help facilitate access to specialised pharmaceutical care. For example, a patient undergoing cancer treatment may need an Oncology Pharmacist with specialised knowledge of chemotherapy and supportive cancer care. A patient with complex neurological conditions may benefit from a Neuropharmacist, while patients with serious infections may need pharmacists specialising in infectious diseases and antimicrobial stewardship. This creates a continuum of pharmaceutical care: Family Pharmacist → Specialist Pharmacist → Multidisciplinary Specialist Care The Family Pharmacist would not replace the physician, nurse, or other healthcare professionals. Instead, the Family Pharmacist would become an important member of the family’s healthcare team, working collaboratively with other professionals to ensure patients receive appropriate pharmaceutical care at the right time. Families could voluntarily engage Family Pharmacists and pay professional fees or subscriptions for agreed services, depending on their healthcare needs and the scope of care provided. This approach could create a sustainable model of personalised pharmaceutical care while recognising pharmacists’ professional value and clinical expertise. Such a model could contribute to addressing major health challenges, including medication errors, adverse drug reactions, drug interactions, polypharmacy, inappropriate self-medication, poor adherence to treatment, irrational use of antibiotics, and medication-related hospital admissions. It could also strengthen preventive healthcare by giving families regular access to a healthcare professional who can identify potential medication-related problems early and provide evidence-based advice before such problems become more serious. As a public health professional and specialist public health pharmacist, I believe Ghana must begin to think beyond the traditional boundaries of healthcare delivery. We must build a preventive, patient-centred, multidisciplinary, accessible, and increasingly personalised healthcare system. The Family Pharmacist concept offers an opportunity to bring pharmaceutical care closer to the family and ensure people have a trusted professional to guide them in the safe, effective use of medicines throughout their lives. Every family should have access to a trusted Family Pharmacist. Every patient with a complex condition should have access to the appropriate specialist pharmacist. Every pharmacist should be empowered to practice at the highest level of their training, competence, and specialisation. Ghana’s healthcare system must evolve towards a model in which the right patient receives the right care from the right healthcare professional at the right time. The future of healthcare is not simply about treating illness after it occurs. It is about prevention, early intervention, personalised care, medication safety, rational use of medicines, and multidisciplinary collaboration. I therefore call for a national conversation among the Ministry of Health, Ghana Health Service, Pharmacy Council, Pharmaceutical Society of Ghana, health insurers, healthcare professionals, policymakers, and the public on developing a sustainable framework for Family Pharmacist services in Ghana. Let us recognise the pharmacist not merely as the professional who dispenses medicines, but as a highly trained healthcare professional and an essential partner in disease prevention, medication safety, health promotion, and the management of complex health conditions. Let us make the Family Pharmacist an essential partner in family healthcare and harness the full potential of specialist pharmacists to build a healthier Ghana. ******* Dr Sheikh Ibrahim Ibn Saana, FGCPharm, MPH

items.title: Mahama to commission 30,000-tonne cashew processing factory in Techiman
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama is expected to commission the Nadkansco Cashew Processing Factory in Techiman on Monday, November 16, in a move aimed at strengthening local agro-processing, creating jobs and increasing Ghana’s export earnings. The facility, financed by the Ghana Export-Import Bank (Ghana EXIM Bank), has the capacity to process approximately 30,000 metric tonnes of cashew annually. It is also expected to operate around the clock to maximise production. Ahead of the commissioning, Ghana EXIM Bank Chief Executive Officer, Sylvester Adinam Mensah, visited the facility to inspect the completed works and assess its readiness to commence operations. Mr Mensah expressed satisfaction with the progress of the project and said the factory had significant potential to stimulate economic activity and provide employment opportunities for residents of Techiman and surrounding communities. The factory is expected to help reduce Ghana’s reliance on exporting raw cashew by processing the commodity locally and increasing its value before it is shipped to international markets. The investment forms part of Ghana EXIM Bank’s broader efforts to promote industrialisation, strengthen the country’s export capacity and generate more foreign exchange through the development of local industries.

items.title: Ghana targets more visa waiver deals by end of 2027 – Ablakwa
items.description: Ghana is pursuing additional visa waiver agreements with countries across the world, with the government expecting to conclude more deals before the end of 2027, Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa has said. He disclosed that Ghana and Tunisia had agreed to commence immediate negotiations on a visa waiver arrangement, as part of broader efforts to make international travel easier for Ghanaian passport holders. In a Facebook post on Sunday, November 15, following a bilateral meeting with Tunisia’s Foreign Affairs Minister, Migration and Tunisians Abroad, Ali Nafti, Mr Ablakwa said several countries had also indicated interest in similar agreements with Ghana. “Last week, Slovakia expressed interest, adding to a growing number of active visa waiver discussions. We expect to sign more Visa Waiver Agreements before the end of 2027,” he stated. Mr Ablakwa said the discussions reflected growing international interest in the Ghanaian passport and reaffirmed the government’s commitment to enhancing its value, prestige and security. Beyond the visa arrangements, the two countries agreed to reactivate their Permanent Joint Commission for Cooperation (PJCC) to provide a framework for strengthening bilateral relations. They also identified education, tourism, sports, agribusiness, trade and maritime affairs as priority areas for collaboration. The Foreign Affairs Minister further said Ghana and Tunisia were considering opening permanent diplomatic missions in each other’s capitals as soon as practicable. He described his engagement with Mr Nafti as meaningful and results-driven and disclosed that he had received an invitation to visit Tunisia.

items.title: EcoNews : Macron et Mushikiwabo, le silence qui arrange Kigali et froisse Kinshasa
Economy Palava: Traders decry rising waybill ‘store keep’ charges
items.description: By Elizabeth Adegbesan Small-scale traders operating across major markets in the country have raised the alarm over arbitrary and escalating storage fees, locally known as “store keep money”, charged by transport operators and motor park agents on delayed waybills, warning that the practice is eroding their capital and threatening their livelihoods. For many market women who rely on interstate commercial buses and trucks to restock goods such as foodstuffs, textiles, and household provisions, waybill logistics are the lifeline of daily commerce. However, traders said the shrinking grace periods before daily demurrage charges kick in have turned routine restocking into a financial burden. Economy&Lifestyle visits to some markets revealed a widespread frustration among traders, many of whom operate on thin profit margins and depend on daily turnover or microfinance loans to sustain their stalls. Mrs. Grace Okafor, a wholesale dealer in dried seafood and condiments, recounted how a 24-hour delay caused by heavy rainfall cost her nearly half of her expected profit on a recent consignment. “My goods arrived at the park late in the evening when no one could go out. “By the time I got there the next afternoon with a tricycle to carry my sacks, the park officials insisted I had exceeded their grace period and demanded N6,000 for ‘store keep’. “We cannot increase our selling prices because customers are already struggling to buy. That money came straight out of my capital.” Other traders noted that the lack of standardized billing across motor parks leaves them vulnerable to exploitation, particularly when unforeseen emergencies delay pickup. Mrs. Comfort Momoh, who trades in fabrics and wrappers, stated that arbitrary fee hikes are discouraging traders from ordering goods in bulk. “There is no fixed rate or clear receipt for this store keep money; it depends on the mood of whoever is on duty at the park store,” she said. “Sometimes a driver does not call on time to inform you that the vehicle has arrived, yet the park starts counting storage days against you. By the time you clear your bale, the profit is already gone.” Similarly, Alhaja Rasheedat Suleiman, a palm oil and grain merchant, called on market associations and transport unions to intervene and establish fair, transparent guidelines. “We understand that parks have limited space, but giving traders at least 48 hours of grace after proper notification is only fair,” Alhaja Suleiman said. “Most of us are breadwinners supporting our families from these stalls. If transport companies and park unions do not regulate these charges, many women will be forced out of business.” When contacted, a park supervisor at an interstate loading bay in, who declined to be named, defended the charges, stating that limited warehouse space and the risk of theft or damage make it necessary to compel traders to clear their goods promptly. This growing extortion racket is more than a minor transport nuisance; it is an informal tax suffocating Nigeria’s micro and small enterprises. Individuals are not left out of this ordeal Mrs. Chidinma Okafor, a tailor, recounted her ordeal saying: “My sister sent me a small carton of clothes from Lagos and paid N4,000 at the park. “When the driver called me, I was already waiting at the terminal. Yet, he refused to bring the bag down from the roof rack until I paid N3,500 for store room and park settlement. “The bag never even touched the ground, let alone entered a store room.” Ibrahim Jato, a baker, said: “I ordered baking ingredients from Onitsha for a weekend wedding cake, and the supplier already cleared the transport fare.” “When I got to the park, three men surrounded the boot and demanded N8,000 for ‘store room security’ before releasing my items. “ When I protested, the driver threatened to lock the boot and return with the goods the next day. “I had no choice but to pay.” Vanguard News The post Economy Palava: Traders decry rising waybill ‘store keep’ charges appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Public parks, playgrounds in Karachi becoming ‘pay-to-play’
items.description: • From indoor cricket to futsal and padel courts, private operators are charging thousands of rupees for use of facilities built on public land • Residents question commercialisation of public spaces • Urge govt to bear maintenance costs instead of handing public facilities to private parties KARACHI: The growing commercialisation of public grounds by the Karachi Metropolitan Corporation (KMC) and Town Municipal Corporations (TMCs) across the metropolis for paid sporting activities has raised concerns about the affordability and accessibility of recreational spaces, particularly for children and young people from low-income households. For instance, there are four playgrounds within a radius of almost one kilometre in a Korangi locality. Yet, children living in the area have limited access to these facilities because they have been put to commercial use and anyone intending to play there has to pay a fee to private operators, raising questions about the very purpose of public recreational spaces meant to serve the needs of citizens. The situation is hardly different in other parts of Karachi, where either the KMC or the TMC concerned have handed over several public playgrounds and parks to private contractors, who make their facilities available to the public only against payment. Dawn visited several areas in different districts of the city and found that multiple public parks and grounds were being used for paid sporting activities, with private operators charging people for access to various facilities. In district Korangi, Rashid Latif Cricket Academy (RLCA) and Eidgah Ground charge Rs6,000 for a three-hour T20 match. Night matches cost around Rs5,000 an hour because generators are used to provide lighting. RLCA, which is run by Landhi TMC, also offers indoor cricket and futsal facilities for Rs3,000 an hour. Umer Sharif Park in Clifton. —Huzaifa Jawaid/Dawn In district South, Umer Sharif Park has eight padel courts, including two of international standard. The hourly charges range between Rs6,000 and Rs10,000 per court. The pickleball area costs Rs3,500 an hour, while the futsal court charges Rs4,000 for a 45-minute session. In district East, HillTop Sports Arena, located inside Hill Park, charges Rs4,000 an hour for indoor cricket and futsal. The rates go up by Rs1,000 on Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays. In district Central, Annu Bhai Cricket Ground in Nazimabad is operated by a private contractor under a KMC contract. A person dealing with the public at the ground said a six-hour daytime booking cost around Rs60,000, while the rate increased to Rs70,000 on Sundays. Night bookings also cost around Rs70,000, partly because of electricity and lighting expenses. At the Mini Sports Complex in Nazimabad No 2, a futsal facility situated on KMC land charges Rs2,500 an hour. At Baloch Mujahid Football Ground in district Malir, charges can reach Rs12,000 for a daytime football match and exceed Rs30,000 at night owing to the additional cost of running generators and fuel. Public access increasingly restricted Residents said the growing use of public spaces for paid sporting activities was making it increasingly difficult for children and young people to participate in sports without having to worry about the cost. Huzaifa Quraishi, the general secretary of Team Mohajir Pakistan, a youth committee based in Korangi, said public grounds were either in poor condition or had been handed over to private parties, leaving ordinary persons with few affordable options. He said providing young people with accessible sporting facilities could also help engage those struggling with drug addiction by giving them opportunities to participate in healthy recreational activities. A resident living near Eidgah Ground in Korangi questioned why a public facility had been developed if children from the neighbourhood could not use it freely. “What good is it when our children cannot play inside it? We could never use it,” the resident said. A former Pakistan national football team player termed the practice of charging people for access to public sporting facilities unethical, saying many players came from modest families and could not afford the fees. He said government departments should bear the cost of maintaining these facilities instead of handing them over to private parties that subsequently charged the public for their use. A woman living near Umer Sharif Park in the South District said residents were unhappy with the way public parks were being managed. She called for parks to be protected from what she described as a “mafia” making excessive profits at residents’ expense. At Hill Park, a family complained that the sporting and play areas were illuminated because they were paid facilities, while the rest of the park remained in darkness. The contrast, they said, reflected the unequal attention being given to commercial facilities and the park’s general recreational spaces. Dawn observed a guard at Eidgah Ground in Korangi scolding children and stopping them from entering the premises to watch a cricket match in progress. When told that it was a public facility and children should not be prevented from entering, he said: “The town chairman has not allowed it. You should ask him.” He added that the public was allowed to enter the ground only between 5pm and 7pm, and only for walking. When contacted, Korangi Town Chairman Naeem Sheikh said the Eidgah ground had been given to a private party for four days a week — from Monday to Thursday. He said the public can access the ground from Friday to Sunday by filing an application. He added that this partial outsourcing model has helped maintain the ground, which has remained in better condition for the past two years. However, he acknowledged that children’s entry is restricted during hardball matches as they could get injured. Authorities justify arrangements A KMC spokesperson said the corporation did not charge users for its facilities available for public use, adding that fees were collected by private parties operating facilities that had been handed over to them by the KMC under contractual arrangements. Responding to concerns about the charges, the spokesperson said contractors set their rates according to prevailing market rates in their respective areas. He added that the KMC was not a price regulatory authority and did not control the rates charged by private contractors. Landhi Town’s Sports Director Muhammad Sohail told Dawn that the charges were intended to cover maintenance and other expenses. “This is not just happening here, but it is normalised across the city,” he said. When contacted, the contractor running Eidgah Ground refused to comment, asking Dawn to reach out to the TMC. The Mini Sports Complex management said it had taken the land from the KMC under a contract and had developed the facilities with its own investment. The representative of Annu Bhai Cricket Ground did not respond to questions, while repeated attempts to contact those operating the facilities at Umer Sharif Park and Hill Park also went unanswered. Published in Dawn, November 16th, 2026

items.title: Ajumako 24-hour economy market 9% complete; traders raise concerns over project location
items.description: The construction of a 24-hour economy market in the Ajumako-Enyan-Essiam District in the Central Region, which commenced in April this year, is progressing steadily, with nine per cent of the work completed. The multi-facility project, scheduled for completion in 24 months, will include commercial buildings housing banks and other businesses, lockable shops, market sheds, an abattoir, food courts, and a fire station, among other facilities. A Ghana News Agency (GNA) visit to the project site at Enyan Abowinum, about five kilometres from Ajumako, the district capital, on Wednesday showed workers on site, with some foundation work underway. Workers cleared part of the four-acre land earmarked for the project to make way for the initial works, while a significant portion, which appeared to be farmland, remained unclear. The GNA also saw granite chippings, an excavator, a concrete mixer, and iron rods at the site. They also drilled a borehole, and a workers’ accommodation facility was under construction. Mr Francis Atinyo, the Project Engineer, told the GNA that construction was currently focused on the lockable shops, which were 12 per cent complete. He noted that excavation was complete; reinforcement mats and column works had been undertaken, with concrete casting scheduled to begin soon, followed by substructure blockwork. He explained that construction of all facilities was expected to run concurrently, but discrepancies in the architectural design had delayed work on most of them. He said the original building designs were larger than the available site, requiring the consultant to revise the plans and adjust the positioning of the structures. He expressed hope that the revised designs would be ready before the end of the week, allowing work to proceed in earnest. That notwithstanding, the engineer maintained that the project remained on schedule, assuring that it would be completed within the stipulated 24 months, provided the government fulfilled its financial obligations. “So far, we are receiving funding regularly, and there is nothing that has hindered that because the certificates that have been raised have been honoured by the clients,” he said. Unlike the Big Push Road projects in the district, Mr Atinyo said the rainy season had not affected their work, and they had not encountered any disputes with landowners. He noted that the project was creating employment and business opportunities for residents, as most labourers came from local communities, with some workers from Accra. Additionally, they sourced some construction materials, including wood, locally. “By December, we should be done with the foundation work for all the buildings so that from January, we will start with the superstructure. By July, at least, some of the commercial buildings should be ready,” the project engineer assured. Meanwhile, some traders in the area have expressed concern about the market’s location and the lack of alternative trading spaces for those being displaced by ongoing road construction. They said Abowinum was relatively far from the district capital, Ajumako, and other communities, making it difficult for traders and customers to access the market. Uncle Fii, a shoe and bag seller, lauding the initiative, said the market would have served traders better if it had been located in the centre of Ajumako, where it would be more accessible to residents of surrounding communities. “It will be difficult for people from Ajumako, Ochiso, Hasowodze and other communities to travel to Abowinum to buy goods. The market should have been located in the centre of town, and so honestly, I do not think the location is suitable,” he said. Uncle further said traders were worried about where they would operate until the new market was completed, as they were being evacuated without compensation to make way for the Big Push project. “Where are we expected to go? Are we supposed to stay at home and watch our families go hungry? We pay three different forms of revenue to the Assembly, so the authorities should treat us fairly. “Officials from the Assembly, together with the road engineer, were here and promised to find us an alternative place to trade. But we still do not know where they are taking us to,” he complained. Nana Afua Abasowah, Adontenhenmaa of Ajumako Abrofoa, also disagreed with the market’s location, describing it as “inconvenient” and appealing for a possible relocation. She said business was already slow, with traders making most of their sales only on Mondays, the main market day. She said the area became heavily congested on market days, with traders displaying goods along the roadside, creating safety risks for both traders and road users. Affected by the Big Push, Nana Abasowah welcomed the road construction but appealed to the authorities to provide alternative trading spaces before evicting traders from their current locations. Another trader, Comfort Baidoo, reiterated that the frequent movement of heavy-duty trucks on the road during construction increased the risk of accidents, particularly when the market became overcrowded. She appealed to the authorities to provide a temporary trading area until the 24-hour economy market was completed. Other traders also called for the speedy completion of the project, saying the lack of permanent trading spaces and slow sales were affecting their livelihoods. Ms Phoebe Akyerefi, a tomato seller from Breman Essiam, urged the Assembly to complete the construction of some stalls at the existing market, which she said had stalled, before embarking on a new one. “As for the 24-hour economy market, the authorities should expedite work to ensure its completion because we are suffering. Our goods are often left to rot because business is slow, and sales are poor,” she said. Madam Esi Attah, a gari and maize seller, also appealed to the government to fulfil its promise to establish a bank for women, saying traders continued to depend on loans with high interest rates to sustain their businesses. Some traders called for improved sanitation in the market and the surrounding towns.

items.title: Nat Tetteh wins NDC Eastern Regional Deputy Secretary position
items.description: Private legal practitioner Nathaniel Guamah Tetteh has been elected Deputy Secretary of the National Democratic Congress (NDC) in the Eastern Region after securing a decisive victory in the party’s regional executive elections. He polled 883 votes out of the 1,012 valid votes cast to defeat his contender, Zakaria Musah, who obtained 126 votes. The results show a margin of 757 votes between the two candidates, with Mr Guamah Tetteh securing approximately 87.3 per cent of the valid votes cast. The election was held on Saturday, November 15, 2026, as delegates of the governing party went to the polls to elect regional executives to steer the party’s affairs in the Eastern Region. Mr Guamah Tetteh’s election places him among the newly elected regional officers responsible for coordinating the party’s administrative activities and supporting its organisational structures in the region.

items.title: Ghana records GHS209.7m in cybersecurity losses in nine months
items.description: Ghana recorded more than GHS209.7 million in financial losses from 4,938 cybersecurity incidents between January and September 2026. The losses exceeded the more than GHS25 million recorded from 4,604 incidents throughout 2025, raising concerns about the security of digital transactions and public confidence in online services. Dr Divine Selase Agbeti, Director-General of the Cyber Security Authority (CSA), disclosed the figures in an address read on his behalf at a cybersecurity industry gathering in Accra. Speaking on the theme, “Architecting Trust in a Digital World,” he said the growing use of mobile money, digital banking, artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and interconnected critical infrastructure has expanded economic opportunities but also increased exposure to cyber threats. Dr Agbeti said trust was essential to the digital economy, adding that confidence would decline if customers feared losing money through mobile money wallets, online fraud, diverted bank transfers or the misuse of personal data without consequences. “When confidence erodes, data adoption slows, businesses lose revenue, financial inclusion suffers, and the broader digital economy weakens,” he said. Dr Agbeti called for a shift from reactive cybersecurity measures to proactive prevention, urging organisations to integrate security into digital systems from the design and development stages. He also urged organisations to strengthen governance and accountability by making cybersecurity a senior-management priority and incorporating it into enterprise risk management systems. Dr Agbeti said institutions should invest in incident response plans, business continuity arrangements, regular security assessments, employee training and recovery systems, noting that no digital environment was completely immune to cyberattacks. Mr Duke Banson, a member of the Ghana Cybersecurity Industry Forum, said stronger collaboration among cybersecurity professionals was necessary to improve the country’s preparedness and resilience. He said the forum was established to bring together professionals from different cybersecurity associations and affiliations to address fragmentation in the industry and build a coordinated national cybersecurity ecosystem. Mr Banson said the forum derived its mandate from the Cybersecurity Act, 2020 (Act 1038), and provided a platform for professionals to exchange ideas, develop industry standards and strengthen Ghana’s cybersecurity capacity. He said the forum had established its governance structure, launched a website and registration portal, and held engagements to encourage professionals to join. Membership was open to students, unemployed persons and established professionals, he said, adding that mentorship programmes would help young people acquire skills to enter the industry. Ms Julia Asante-Mensah, Vice-President of the Women in CyberSecurity (WiCyS) West Africa Affiliate, said growing dependence on digital technologies made it important for individuals and organisations to understand the risks associated with the systems they used. She cited disruption to Microsoft Teams and Outlook services as an example of how problems with a major technology platform could affect users and organisations globally. Mrs Asante-Mensah said technological advancement should be matched by responsible digital behaviour, collaboration and deliberate efforts to develop secure systems. She urged participants to help strengthen the digital ecosystem and pursue careers in technology out of genuine interest and commitment, not just because of its growing popularity.

Without manufacturing $1trn economy is an illusion
items.description: By Dele Sobowale Japan in fact offers a relevant historical example of what can happen to an economy which falls behind in the global manufacturing race. Even in Africa, the Giant of Africa is lagging behind at least three other economies in the scale and scope of manufacturing. Consequently, the politically-motivated promise to make Nigeria a one trillion dollar economy by 2030 is only one of the many illusions of the Tinubu administration. Desirable as it is, a $1 trillion economy is unachievable for reasons too numerous to discuss now, but, the cardinal reason is Nigeria’s weak manufacturing base – forcing us to import thousands of products which we can, with little effort, produce locally. I was a Senior Lecturer/Consultant working with the Nigerian Institute of Management, NIM, in 1992, when Morita wrote the article in which that statement was made. The NIM Library was my second home and office. When not busy teaching courses in Sales, Marketing and General Management, I was in the Library reading and gathering materials for my lectures, as well as my book of quotations, VBQ – which was published in 2007. Japan was the world’s second largest manufacturing economy as well as the second largest economy; and was threatening the American leadership in that regard. Several books were written on the Art of Japanese Management; leading American Business Schools included courses in Japanese business methods in their curricula as compulsory subjects. The Japanese economy was growing at 7 to 10 per cent annually; and projections were made regarding when it would overtake the US as the largest economy globally. China and India were nowhere in sight. Then, something happened. Science and technology brought new products which called for new and modern factories. Western investors, scared by Japan’s growing economic prowess, diverted investments to other Asian economies – South Korea, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and China. Gradually, several South East Asian nations started challenging Japan in sectors such as electronics and ship building. Unnoticeable at first, but the steady erosion of Japanese share of global manufacturing eventually took its toll. Today, the second and third leading manufacturers are China and India. China is now the largest manufacturer; hotly pursued by China. Japan has dropped to the fifth position in global ranking measured in terms of Gross Domestic Productivity, GDP. China, not Japan, is now threatening the US leadership. Manufacturing is the primary reason for that change in the fortunes of nations. Nigeria Is Missing The Boat Once Again “Those who do not remember the past are condemned to repeat it.” – George Santayana, 1863-1952, VBQ p 93. It might be difficult for the Generation Z youths to believe that Nigeria once embarked on rapid industrialization. The Gowon administration sent delegations to the United States in 1974 to appeal to young and well-educated Nigerians to return home and fill vacant positions opening up in manufacturing in several industrial layouts in Lagos, Ibadan, Kaduna, Kano, Portharcourt and Aba. I was one of those who responded to the call to return home and help Nigeria’s transformation to a manufacturing giant. On arrival in August 1974, my first working experience was at the Ilupeju Industrial Layout in Lagos. I soon discovered there were others in Lagos State – Ikeja, Iganmu and Apapa. My first trip to Portharcourt and Aba revealed the Trans Amadi and Ogbor Hill layouts respectively; the Northern legs of the national familiarization tour took me to Kano’s Bompai, Kaduna and Anglo Jos in Plateau state. Granted, everything I saw could not have been more than a few establishments on Route 128, Massachusetts, USA – where I gained industrial experience. But it was a promising start. Construction of new factories and expansion of old factories was going on at feverish pace. Jobs were available everywhere. I left manufacturing enterprises in 1990 after working in five different industrial layouts. The last was in Kalambina, Sokoto State. Unfortunately, the 16 years between 1974 and 1990 represented the period of the rise and decline of manufacturing in Nigeria. Instead of building on what we started, gradual decline set in. SPARS, a retail outlet, has replaced our factory for analgesics and cough syrup. The brewery in Bompai lies in ruins; and the rice mill in Sokoto remains shut since 1991. Right now, the current reforms embarked upon by President Tinubu threaten to again set in motion the process which made manufacturing extremely difficult in Nigeria. Current Situation: No Power; Expensive Credit “Power supply plunges as gas shortage, water level worsen.” VANGUARD, November 6, 2026 Manufacturing became very attractive in the 1970s when the Kainji Hydro Power Station was established. None of the industrial estates could have been started without relatively reliable public power supply. Definitely, Nigerian Paper Mill, Jeba; Nigerian Sugar Company, NISUCO and the Nigerian Yeast and Alcohol Manufacturing Company, both at Bacita, Kwara State could not have been started if they had to operate on generators. I was a consultant for the three; and I recall the discussions with their Chief Executive Officers. Without exception, they were certain their companies could not survive on generators. They were absolutely correct. On November 5, 2026, Nigeria was able to supply only 2,926MW to the entire nation. That is deeply concerning for two reasons. One, we achieved capacity to generate 4,000MW per day as far back as 2012. Fourteen years later, the Federal Government is still offering the same excuses for remaining stuck at 4,000MW on a good day. No $1 trillion economy generates less than 45,000MW. South Africa is Africa’s largest economy, far less than the $1 trillion economy. But, it already provides more than 45,000MW. “Banks’ loan to manufacturers slumps 26.8% to N5.19trn.” VANGUARD, October 26, 2026. Credit is the soul of business and has been an axiom for several hundred years. Banks and financial institutions were established primarily to promote businesses; not to finance government deficits. The Great Depression in the last century, as well as the rise of Keynesianism, gave rise to governments invading banks to borrow funds for their operations. Deficit spending, once proposed as a short-term measure, has hardened into a permanent feature of fiscal policy. Very few governments now attempt to balance their budgets. Reliance on deficit spending and perpetual borrowing is the new normal. In the process, banks are increasingly called upon to extend credits to the government. Private sector borrowers, especially manufacturers are bearing the brunt of the new situation. Nigerian manufacturers are being hammered three ways. First, they don’t receive as much as they would want. Second, the interest rates are exorbitant. Third, they compete against foreign producers whose governments provide support across the board and whose banks charge single digit interest rates. How we expect Nigerian manufacturers paying 30 per cent to compete with Chinese paying 2 per cent remains a mystery to me. Follow me on Facebook @ J Israel Biola Vanguard News The post Without manufacturing $1trn economy is an illusion appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Ablakwa highlights Mahama’s Volta projects
items.description: Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, Member of Parliament (MP) for North Tongu, has described the Volivo bridge construction and the 12,000-capacity FIFA-standard stadium in the Volta region as a big push for the development of the region. Speaking at the National Democratic Congress (NDC) Volta Regional Delegates Conference in Ho on Saturday, he said the 2027 budget presented to parliament showed the President’s commitment to the development of the region. “I am so excited that the long-awaited Volivo Bridge, which goes through my constituency, my beloved North Tongu, is announced to receive a massive allocation of GH¢400 million in the 2027 budget” Mr Ablakwa said the President had declared that 10 regions would receive a modern FIFA-standard stadium, with the Volta Region receiving the biggest, with a 12,000-seat capacity. He also recalled President Mahama’s campaign promise to the people of Ketu South for a modern multi-purpose market, noting that a US$30 million grant had been secured from China for the new Aflao market. Mr Ablakwa said the principles and values of the founder of the Party, former President Rawlings, remained a guiding principle for the party and “we are so proud that in our current President Mahama, we see those principles, those values, every single day in this administration.” The Foreign Affairs Minister therefore cautioned against distraction, saying the agenda of opponents these days was to fabricate, concoct, engage in smear campaigns and character assassination. “They know that we are doing well on the economy, in infrastructure, we are delivering on our promises, and we are leading with integrity, so all they want to do now is to target some of us by engaging in vicious vilification, but they will fail, because the truth always stands, and the truth shall always vindicate us.” The conference, which elected regional executives of the party to be at the helm of affairs for the next four years, had in attendance the General Secretary of the NDC, Ministers, Volta Region’s Representative on the Council of State, MPs, and a representation of Volta Regional Executives of the opposition New Patriotic Party.

items.title: Tourisme : la Tunisie vise une clientèle plus riche que les Algériens et les Libyens
items.description: Le nombre de touristes qui ont visité la Tunisie n’a pas cessé de croître ces dernières années. Mais le gouvernement ne semble pas très satisfait par la qualité de ces touristes qui ne dépense pas assez d’argent. La Tunisie veut changer la donne pour viser une clientèle plus riche. Les Maghrébins, Algériens et les Libyens notamment, qui constituent la moitié du flux touristique de cette destination, ne rapportent pas assez pour le secteur touristique tunisien. La Tunisie veut séduire des touristes au pouvoir d’achat élevé À fin octobre 2026, les recettes touristiques de la Tunisie ont atteint 7,152 milliards TND (environ 2,3 milliards de $). Ce montant marque une croissance de 3,4 % par rapport à la même période de 2025 et plus 25% par rapport à 2019, note le ministre tunisien du Tourisme, Sofiène Tekaya, devant l’Assemblée de représentants du peuple (ARP). Selon lui, la Consommation intérieure globale a atteint 17,47 milliards TND en 2025, contre 16,1 milliards en 2024 et 14,6 milliards en 2023. La consommation des visiteurs non résident, c’est-à-dire les dépenses des touristes en hébergement, transport, achat de biens et de services, est estimée à 12,8 milliards TND. Les visiteurs résidents ont dépensé, quant à eux, 4,7 milliards TND. Plus de 64 % des recettes touristiques enregistrées en 2025 sont générées par des touristes en provenance d’Europe, la France en tête, suivi de l’Allemagne, l’Italie et le Royaume-Uni. Sofiène Tekaya a indiqué devant les membres du Parlement que les ambitions de la Tunisie ne se « limitent plus à attirer un nombre croissant » de visiteurs mais consiste également à améliorer la « rentabilité » et à « séduire une clientèle disposant d’un pouvoir de dépense élevé ». L’objectif est d'accroître la valeur ajoutée, les revenus des établissements touristiques et la contribution du secteur à l’économie du pays, a-t-il dit, selon la presse locale. Des dépenses touristiques faibles Le même responsable avait indiqué, début novembre, qu’entre le 1 er janvier et le 20 octobre 2026, la Tunisie a enregistré 8,69 millions d’arrivées de visiteurs non-résidents. Les postes frontaliers tunisiens ont enregistré, à la même date, 3,98 visiteurs algériens et libyens, soit 50,1 % des entrées de non-résidents. Selon le directeur général de l’Office tunisien du tourisme, plus de 2,25 millions d’Algériens ont visité la Tunisie, entre janvier et le 10 septembre 2026. Selon un calcul fait par le site spécialisé Voyages & Diaspora sur la base des 11 millions de visiteurs de 2025 pour une recette totale de 8.096,9 millions de dinars, un touriste dépense en moyenne 250 dollars en Tunisie, ce qui est considéré comme faible. L’article Tourisme : la Tunisie vise une clientèle plus riche que les Algériens et les Libyens est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: UAE: 5 Shia Residents Arrested Arbitrarily
items.description: Click to expand Image Abu Dhabi Court House Complex, Dar Al-Omran, Abu Dhabi, UAE, February 2017. © 2017 Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty Images (Beirut) – Emirati authorities have arbitrarily detained at least five Shia Muslim foreign residents since the United States and Israel carried out military strikes on Iran in February 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. The detentions appear to be based on the detainees’ religious identity. Emirati authorities detained the residents, who had been in the UAE between 2 and 40 years, between March and May. They have not been brought before a judge or formally charged, three informed sources said. “Emirati authorities appear to be rounding up residents simply based on their religious beliefs as Shia Muslims in a largely Sunni country rather than providing any evidence of wrongdoing, while trampling over people’s due process rights,” said Joey Shea, senior UAE researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The authorities should immediately release anyone targeted because of their religion.” Between September and October, Human Rights Watch interviewed the three sources and reviewed CCTV footage of a raid on the company that one of the detainees owned. The detainees’ and sources’ names are withheld for fear of reprisals against them and their relatives. The sources said that security authorities asked at least one of the detainees about his religious affiliation before his arrest and interrogated at least one family member about their religious views. Another Shia community member warned at least one detainee and a relative to leave the UAE. On March 23, Emirati state security arrested one man, 44, in Sharjah, as he was in his car near his home at midnight, a relative said. He was not allowed to contact a lawyer or his family that night. The following night, Emirati security forces took the man to his family home for a search. The officers took money, jewelry, books, and credit cards, his relative said. Security forces did not inform him or his family of any charges against him. The relative said that a worker at the mosque they attended had warned him to leave the country in June 2025. The government “viewed us Shias as sleeper cells,” he said. The relative left the UAE two days later. The same mosque worker asked the man on March 20, 2026, whether he had “any problems with the police.” The relative said this was how the man had been warned, but he did not understand it as a warning and stayed in the UAE. Emirati security forces also raided the man’s company. Human Rights Watch reviewed CCTV footage reportedly from the site, timestamped March 24. The footage shows two men, one in a baseball cap and the other in traditional clothing, entering the man’s company at around 9:19 p.m. and searching offices. One enters a room with computers and appears to tamper with the equipment. The man was held in incommunicado detention for three days, then allowed to make a one-minute call to his family. He has been allowed two-minute calls every two weeks since. Prison authorities end the call if he attempts to reveal information about his case or location. His family has not been allowed to visit. On September 14, the family learned through his lawyer that he had been moved to the notorious al-Sadr prison in Abu Dhabi, the source said. Emirati authorities have held the prominent Emirati human rights defender Ahmed Mansour there since 2017 in conditions that may amount to torture. On the evening of April 22, state security officials arrested a 38-year-old foreign Shia national at a money transfer office near his home in Sharjah, a relative said. They took him to his home and searched it, seizing money, gold jewelry, and his laptop without informing his family of any charges. On May 29, Emirati authorities summoned his wife for questioning, including about her husband’s religious views, the source said. Authorities released her at 10 a.m. on May 30. Emirati authorities held him in incommunicado detention, allowing him to make a brief call on June 3, the source said. Authorities allow him one brief phone call every week in which he cannot reveal the details of his detention. The authorities told his wife on October 6 that he had been moved to al-Sadr prison. She has not been allowed to visit him. Emirati authorities arrested three more foreign Shia nationals between April and May, a third source related to the men said. Security forces raided the homes of all three men, confiscated their passports and money, and did not inform them of the charges against them, the source said. During one of the raids, a security officer asked a family member about their religion, job, and income, the source said. Before the arrest, one of the men received a phone call from Emirati authorities asking about a religious issue and the names of his associates, the source said. The three men have been allowed to make a brief call every ten days without revealing their location, the source said. Prison authorities end the call if they attempt to give details about the case or detention conditions. “We all left the UAE in one day,” a family member said. “We wrapped up over 30 years in the UAE… We gave the UAE our hopes, dreams, and children, then they betrayed us like this. We sang their national anthem in schools. We loved this country and it betrayed us.” Human Rights Watch has previously documented Emirati authorities arbitrarily detaining and forcibly disappearing and expelling other Shia residents, without due process, between 2009 and 2021. Reuters reported that thousands of Pakistani Shia residents have been deported from Gulf Arab states since February 28. During the same period, Emirati authorities revoked visas of Iranian families who have lived in the UAE for decades and banned Iranian nationals from transiting through the UAE, media and UAE Foreign Ministry reports said. On February 28, the United States and Israel carried out airstrikes on Iran, and Iran retaliated with strikes against Israel and Gulf states. Iran has since launched thousands of drones and missiles at Gulf countries, with the largest number striking the UAE. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International found that Gulf governments responded by intensifying restrictions on the rights to freedom of expression, association, and peaceful assembly during the conflict, in an already repressive environment. Under international law, governments have a responsibility to protect public safety in wartime, but security measures must be lawful, necessary, proportionate, and nondiscriminatory. Detaining people because of their religion and holding them without charge and access to lawyers is never justified, Human Rights Watch said. “Emirati authorities should not treat the Shia community as a security threat in response to Iran’s unlawful strikes on the UAE,” Shea said.

items.title: Joyce Bawah Mogtari hails NDC’s democratic process, expresses confidence in party’s future
items.description: Senior Aide and Advisor to President John Mahama, Joyce Bawah Mogtari, has expressed renewed confidence in the National Democratic Congress (NDC) ‘s future following the successful organisation of the party’s constituency and regional elections. In a Facebook post, she said observing the party’s internal electoral process as a member, senior foot soldier, and keen observer, rather than as a contestant, gave her a fresh appreciation of the NDC’s democratic culture. She noted that the experience had also rekindled fond memories of her late father and the significant role he played in the party’s internal elections. Mrs Bawah Mogtari described genuine decentralisation as fundamental to the growth and sustainability of Ghana’s democracy, arguing that the NDC represents a progressive and modern model of democratic practice from which other political organisations could learn. She congratulated the victors and commended all unsuccessful aspirants for their courage, commitment, and contribution to strengthening the party’s democratic process. As the NDC prepares to elect its national officers next month, she urged members to set aside their differences and prioritise the party’s collective interest. “No individual victory is greater than the collective success of our party,” she stated, stressing that the NDC’s strength lies in its unity and shared vision. She added that every member has a responsibility to protect the party’s democratic values and advance the ideals upon which it was founded. “Ultimately, we are all winners, and we should remain proud members of the great Umbrella family,” she said.
