items.title: Moroccan Sahara: France reiterates ‘unwavering’ position in support of Morocco’s sovereignty and of autonomy
items.description: France reiterated on Friday its “unwavering” position that “the present and future of Western Sahara fall within the framework of Moroccan sovereignty,” according to a statement from the spokesperson for the French Ministry of Europe and Foreign Affairs. Issued after a meeting in Essaouira between Minister of Foreign Affairs, African Cooperation, and Moroccan Expatriates Nasser Bourita and his French counterpart Jean-Noël Barrot, the statement emphasises that Morocco’s 2007 autonomy plan is “the only basis for reaching a just, lasting, and negotiated political solution.” The French minister also called for continued dialogue, renewing his support for the United Nations’ efforts based on Resolution 2797. The statement also notes that Barrot and Bourita took stock of the “exceptional and reinforced partnership” between France and Morocco, nearly two years after the President of the Republic’s State visit to Morocco, made at the invitation of His Majesty King Mohammed VI. In this context, the two ministers discussed the many areas where France-Morocco relations are experiencing a “particularly fruitful momentum,” welcoming the prospect of concluding a bilateral France-Morocco treaty. According to the same source, the two ministers also discussed regional and international issues of mutual interest, particularly the situation in the Near and Middle East and the Sahel, with Barrot reaffirming his commitment to using France-Morocco cooperation to help resolve crises.

items.title: Separate legislative assembly in Islamabad on the cards
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The government has intensified its efforts to set up a separate legislative assembly in Islamabad. If all goes as planned, a legislative assembly will be set up in the capital city, which will be headed by an elected mayor. Some months ago, a high-profile committee headed by Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal had finalised recommendations, which were presented to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. The recommendations proposed the devolution of powers from the federation to Islamabad Capital Territory as a federating unit, with a provincial-style government. It was stated that the proposed Islamabad Assembly would have 27 members and would be headed by an elected mayor/chief minister. However, new proposals are now emerging for setting up a separate legislative assembly. Some TV channels reported on Sunday that the boundaries of Islamabad would also be expanded and that there were chances that Haripur, Murree and parts of Rawalpindi would be made part of Islamabad. When contacted, a senior government officer said that it was clear that a new, separate legislative assembly would be set up in Islamabad. “As far as making Haripur, Rawalpindi and Murree part of Islamabad is concerned, nothing is final yet. They are part of separate provinces, and we will see if they can be made part of Islamabad or how laws passed by Islamabad will be implemented in these areas. So, again, nothing is final; these are discussions. But yes, Islamabad will have a separate legislative assembly,” he said. It is relevant to note here that local government elections in Islamabad have been facing inordinate delays, as the elections have been postponed at least five times during the last four years, with the government always stating that new legislation is being made for a “vibrant system”. As per the latest schedule, elections were supposed to be held on Dec 20, but the Islamabad High Court suspended the schedule on a petition which pleaded that polls could not be held until the legal status of the existing constituency delimitation was conclusively determined. Published in Dawn, November 16th, 2026

items.title: Crisis hits Nigeria’s cassava industry with imports rising 13,293% in 5yrs
items.description: *… as Farmers Abandon Farms in 2026 By Cynthia Alo Nigeria’s cassava processing industry is facing a deepening crisis as imports of cassava starch surged by 13,293 per cent in five years, leaving local factories struggling, farmers counting their losses and processors operating at low 15 per cent of their installed capacity. This is happening despite Nigeria’s position as the world’s largest cassava producer as of 2024, according to the Food and Agriculture Organization Corporate Statistical Database, FAOSTAT, an agency of the United Nations. Industry stakeholders attributed the crisis to high production costs, inadequate financing, declining farm acreage and weak enforcement of import restrictions. These factors have made imported alternatives cheaper than locally produced cassava derivatives. The situation has resulted in a glut of raw cassava, falling farm-gate prices, mounting debts among farmers and processors, and growing concerns about the future of local industrial production. Data obtained from the World Bank’s World Integrated Trade Solution, WITS, based on UN Comtrade records, showed that Nigeria’s cassava starch imports rose from 24.1 tonnes in 2020 to 3,227.7 tonnes in 2025, representing a 13,293 per cent increase over five years. A year-on-year breakdown showed that Nigeria imported 24.1 tonnes of cassava starch, valued at $69,440, in 2020. Imports increased by 126.6 per cent year-on-year (YoY) in 2021 to 54.6 tonnes, worth $154,750. In 2022, the volume surged by a further 272.2 per cent YoY to 203.2 tonnes, valued at $292,900. However, following a sharp rise in the exchange rate, imports plunged by 98 per cent YoY in 2023 to 4.1 tonnes, valued at $32,080, before rebounding sharply in 2024 by 73,004.9 per cent to 2,997.3 tonnes, worth $2.34 million. The upward trend continued in 2025, with import volumes rising by 7.7 per cent to 3,227.7 tonnes. However, despite the increase in volume, the value of imports declined by 7.6 per cent to $2.16 million from approximately $2.34 million in 2024. Industry stakeholders, who spoke in exclusive interviews with Financial Vanguard, warned that imports were rising further in 2026 and could continue to increase in subsequent years unless the government addressed the cost disadvantages confronting local processors and strengthened policies supporting domestic production. Farmers, processors count losses The President of Large-Scale Starch and Derivatives Producers Association of Nigeria, LSSDPA, Mrs Oluyemisi Iranloye, who is also the Vice-President of the Industrial Cassava Stakeholders Association of Nigeria, ICSAN, said the crisis had severely affected farmers and processors. Iranloye, founder and Chief Executive Officer of Psaltry International, said farmers could spend about N800,000 cultivating a hectare of cassava but realise only about N300,000 from selling the produce at prevailing farm-gate prices. She said the situation had discouraged farmers from planting, while industrial processors, which ordinarily absorb substantial quantities of cassava, were scaling down operations because of weak demand. Illustrating crisis severity in the processing industry, she said: “As you speak right now, factories that should be generating about N10 billion a year are barely generating N1 billion. Factories are running at about 15 per cent capacity because there’s no market. “The market that is available is flooded by importation. So factories are dying, people cannot pay up their loans. We buy from smallholder farmers, and when we are not buying, smallholder farmers cannot sell, and the implication is that everybody suffers. “What we have witnessed over the last 18 to 20 months is particularly troubling. Several processing companies have either reduced their operations, struggled to maintain production or become less active in the market. “Consequently, the volume of cassava that would ordinarily have been absorbed by industrial processors has increasingly remained within the traditional food market, putting considerable pressure on farm-gate prices.” Iranloye warned that the situation could also threaten future cassava supplies as farmers become increasingly reluctant to invest in cultivation when they cannot recover their production costs. She said the solution laid in addressing the broader production and supply-chain constraints. “We must also invest in the agricultural supply base, mechanisation, improved planting materials, aggregation centres, transportation and alternative energy solutions,” she said. Tariff favours imports Explaining the factors behind the growing dependence on imported starch, Iranloye said the current tariff structure had made imported corn starch and pharmaceutical-grade starch cheaper than locally produced cassava starch. According to her, the reduction in tariffs on competing products, such as corn starch and pharmaceutical-grade starch, had made imported alternatives more competitive than locally produced cassava starch She said: “I believe this report, the imports will increase in 2026 because the import duty is still supporting cassava starch and corn starch, a situation that large-scale starch and its derivative producers have been fighting. “Now, the situation is that the tariff on corn starch used to be about 15 per cent some four years ago, and at that point, we were able to compete because we had some form of little protection. “But right now, the tariff on corn starch and pharmaceutical-grade starch were reduced to five per cent. What it means is that they can bring it in cheaper than what we are producing. “So, the multinationals that usually buy from us, the large-scale starch factories in Nigeria, are now importing, landing cheaper than our cost of production, so they now import thousands of containers, and they now buy very little locally. “The implication is that we are also not buying much cassava from farmers, so prices have crashed below what the farmers can handle, and that’s why we have the glut right now.” Iranloye said pharmaceutical-grade starch was also being brought into Nigeria under zero-duty arrangements, with some importers allegedly importing quantities beyond their immediate requirements and selling the excess in the local market. She said: “Another point is pharmaceutical-grade starch also finds its way into Nigeria. So pharmaceutical companies are importing pharmaceutical-grade starch into Nigeria at zero duty. “But instead of just importing the quantity that they require alone, they import more and sell also to the local market. “So we have been fighting the importation heavily, yet we have more than 30 factories not running well, cassava not being bought, there’s glut because of tariff mismatch.” The Federal Government’s Executive Order on Increasing Local Production of Healthcare Products provides import-duty and VAT exemptions for specified pharmaceutical raw materials. The official list of exempted materials specifically includes pharmaceutical-grade corn starch under HS Code 1108121000. Farmers warn of further supply decline Meanwhile, food security expert and farmer, Mr Africanfarmer Mogaji, said Nigeria could continue to experience increased importation in 2026, particularly through less-publicised channels, if government policies remained inconsistent. Mogaji said Nigeria had significantly expanded its cassava processing capacity over the past decade, particularly as foreign exchange pressures made imports more expensive and encouraged manufacturers to source raw materials locally. However, he said many farmers and processors who invested during that period are now heavily indebted following changes in market conditions. He said: “The processors have increased capacity by taking loans because of the demand previously. The farmers have taken loans, taken too much risk, over-exposed themselves. “And now it is cheaper to import cassava starch from Thailand because the government of that country has heavily invested in infrastructure from raw material to inputs to logistics. “So many of the multinationals have over-imported and they are not taking the starch from the Nigerian processors, and so the processors also cannot take cassava from the local farmers.” Mogaji said some multinational companies had taken advantage of import windows to bring in quantities beyond their immediate requirements, thereby weakening demand for locally produced cassava derivatives. He said the impact could persist beyond 2026 because some manufacturers had already secured imported supplies for an extended period. He said: “They’ve secured themselves mostly till the end of 2027 and first quarter 2028. “So Nigerians will feel it on their table again. And so whatever government is trying to do to tighten up to support local production will be a waste.” Mogaji said Nigeria needs a long-term agricultural policy framework that will enable farmers and processors to plan beyond individual administrations. He said: “If we don’t have policies that can last an average of 10 years in the pilot stage, we’re not going anywhere. “But we can convert and focus on food, maybe cassava to fufu, cassava to garri, cassava to paste, cassava to many other products that people can consume at scale. “I’m optimistic there’s still room for the private sector, but over-dependence on government would not work.” Farmers reduce acreage as costs rise Similarly, the Managing Director of Niji Group, Mr Kolawole Adeniji, said the projected increase in imports in 2026 will also be driven by a decline in cassava farming activities this year. Adeniji, who has more than 36 years of experience in agriculture and operates a cassava farm covering more than 4,000 acres, said farmers were reducing farm sizes because of the high costs of machinery, diesel and transportation, insecurity, and poor returns on cassava cultivation. He said: “The import will increase next year because a lot of people are not farming this year. Farmers have reduced the acreage of their farm sizes due to the implements and the cost of tractors, insecurity, then the poor market for what they have planted over a period of three years. “So a lot of people are not doing any serious farming this year. The cost of diesel is very high, so the cost of transportation is very high. The cost of selling tractors, when you look at all the factors surrounding the production, people are not farming the way they should. So it’s going to affect us next year.” Adeniji also attributed Nigeria’s dependence on imported starch to the high cost of producing and processing cassava locally, saying farmers and processors faced expenses that producers in competing countries do not bear to the same extent. He said: “Most of the farmers who are practising are not making profit because the supporting system is not properly structured.” According to him, imported starch, including potato and maize starch, can also be cheaper than locally produced cassava starch because of differences in infrastructure, energy and production costs. He said: “Immediately the government opened the border to bring starch, the cost of producing potato starch and everything is cheaper than what you produce in Nigeria.” Adeniji also said cassava processing required long-term financing, arguing that farmers and processors could not operate sustainably with short-term loans. He said: “If the government wants to provide loans, it must be almost a three year cycle.” Processing capacity struggles despite investment Despite the challenges, industry records showed that Nigeria has developed significant cassava processing capacity over the years. A June 18, 2026, document obtained by Vanguard from the Large-Scale Starch and Derivatives Producers Association listed 62 cassava processor entries affiliated with the association, including processors registered with ICSAN. The records showed that 55 entries were engaged in starch and high-quality cassava flour, HQCF, processing, with a combined listed daily capacity of 1,662.5 tonnes, while seven ethanol-related processors had a combined recorded capacity of 1.073 million litres daily. Among the companies listed for starch and HQCF production were Psaltry International Limited, Dufil Prima Foods Limited, GreenTech Industries Limited, Harvest Feed and Agro Processing Limited, Niji Industries Limited, Acsmin Cassava Industries and Premium Cassava Product Limited. The ethanol processors included Green Hills Agricultural Products, Premier Plantations Limited, Weewood Industries Limited, Allied Atlantic Distilleries Limited, Pure Biotech Company Limited, Unicane Industries Limited and Arog BioAllied Agro Services Limited. However, the association noted that some companies might not be operating at full capacity because of challenges, while some companies, including those operated by Chinese investors, were not captured in the list. Production versus industrial use The concerns come despite Nigeria’s position as the world’s largest cassava producer. Data from the Food and Agriculture Organization Corporate Statistical Database, FAOSTAT, released in 2025, showed that Nigeria accounted for about 18 per cent of global cassava output in 2024, ahead of the Democratic Republic of Congo and Ghana, while national production had risen to more than 63 million tonnes. However, the country’s large production volume has not translated into commensurate industrial utilisation. Speaking at the 10th anniversary of ICSAN in Lagos, its President, Mr Segun Ladele, said only about five per cent of Nigeria’s cassava output currently goes into industrial use, with the bulk consumed as food or exported. He said: “About 80 per cent is consumed locally as food, five per cent goes into industry and about 15 per cent for export. So when we are talking about industrialisation, there is still a lot of room to make improvements.” Vanguard News The post Crisis hits Nigeria’s cassava industry with imports rising 13,293% in 5yrs appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Ghana receives up to 62 tonnes of mercury annually through illicit channels
items.description: Ghana receives between 42.5 and 62 tonnes of mercury annually through illicit channels for use in artisanal and small-scale gold mining, stakeholders have disclosed. The continued use of the toxic substance in mining communities poses risks to water resources, the environment and public health, they said. Dr Sylvester Akpah, Chief Executive Officer of Smart Innovation Ghana Limited, disclosed this at a symposium organised by the United States Embassy in Accra on behalf of the Regional Environment, Science, Technology and Health Hub for West and Central Africa under the Ambassador’s Water Experts Programme. He said the mercury entered the country through unidentified routes and was used in artisanal and small-scale mining communities. Dr Akpah said more than 2.5 million people depended directly or indirectly on small-scale mining for their livelihoods, making the uncontrolled use of mercury a major concern. He said mining communities in the Western, Ashanti, Eastern and Central regions were particularly affected by mercury pollution, with a number of water bodies contaminated. Dr Akpah identified Tarkwa and surrounding communities as areas under severe environmental pressure and said continued pollution could threaten access to safe drinking water. He said mercury continued to enter the country through illicit channels despite existing controls at the ports. Dr Akpah also cited the absence of a dedicated national directorate to oversee mercury use and related controls in the mining sector as a challenge to effective regulation. He said miners and residents of nearby communities faced exposure through the routine use of mercury in gold-processing activities, which could affect the kidneys, lungs and brain. Dr Akpah called for stricter enforcement of existing regulations and the adoption of technologies to reduce and eventually eliminate mercury use in small-scale mining. He cited gold-catching technologies as an alternative but said their adoption remained limited despite investments in importing the equipment. Dr Akpah noted that Ghana had ratified the Minamata Convention on Mercury, an international agreement aimed at protecting human health and the environment from mercury pollution, but said enforcement remained a challenge. Professor Daniel Nukpezah of the Institute for Environment and Sanitation Studies, University of Ghana, said mercury pollution required stronger surveillance and management systems. He said mercury was a toxic heavy metal that did not break down in the environment but moved through air, water, soil, sediments and living organisms. Prof. Nukpezah said mercury could be transformed into methylmercury in aquatic environments, where it accumulated in fish and entered the human food chain. He explained that bacteria in sediments converted mercury deposited in water bodies into methylmercury, which was absorbed by aquatic organisms. Prof. Nukpezah said mercury concentrations increased as larger fish consumed smaller organisms, thereby increasing human exposure through the food chain. He said exposure could occur through inhalation of contaminated air, consumption of polluted water and fish, contact with contaminated soil and participation in mining activities. Prof. Nukpezah identified artisanal and small-scale gold mining as a major source of mercury pollution in Ghana because miners used the substance as a relatively inexpensive means of extracting gold from ore. He also identified electronic waste processing and other industrial activities as sources of mercury contamination. Citing findings from the United Nations Environment Programme, Prof. Nukpezah said atmospheric mercury concentrations had increased by about 450 per cent above natural levels. He said mercury occurred in different chemical forms, each presenting varying levels of risk, and called for appropriate sampling and testing to determine the extent of contamination. Prof. Nukpezah urged the development of local capacity to monitor mercury pollution and exposure. He said effective interventions required a better understanding of mercury sources, its movement through the environment and the pathways through which it entered human populations. The symposium sought to identify measures to reduce mercury use and promote environmentally sustainable mining practices. The two-day forum brought together government officials, academics, civil society organisations, development partners and private-sector representatives to discuss measures to address mercury pollution and protect Ghana’s water resources.

items.title: Historic Malot Fort in Chakwal presents a picture of neglect
items.description: From a distance, Malot Fort looks like a postcard. Perched on a hilltop in the picturesque Salt Range near Kallar Kahar, the historic monument offers breathtaking views of the surrounding landscape. As visitors climb the hill, the Malot Temple comes into view, standing alone against the vast sky. On a clear day, the River Jhelum can also be seen from the fort. For a moment, the visitor may believe the promotional video circulating on Facebook that describes the site as “Punjab’s undiscovered heritage jewel”. But the experience changes as one approaches the fort. The road disappears into scattered stones, while thorny kikri (Prosopis juliflora) bushes encroach on the pathway. Parthenium, one of the most invasive weeds, has spread across the complex. Newly installed benches lie broken, and a half-built structure stands abandoned. A newly-installed bench lies broken at Malot Fort, reflecting the lack of maintenance at the historic site. Inside the fort, donkeys and cattle graze and rest in areas meant for tourists. Mobile phone companies have also installed towers beside the thousand-year-old monument, creating a strange juxtaposition of modern infrastructure and historic heritage. Described as the most beautiful fort in the Salt Range, Malot has been the subject of two consecutive projects undertaken by the Punjab Archaeology Department and the Tourism Development Corporation of Punjab (TDCP) for its conservation, restoration and development. Despite these initiatives, toilets have yet to be constructed, development work has been halted due to a shortage of funds, and animal waste is scattered across the premises. The fort and village of Malot are named after Raja Mal or Mallu, the first ruler and ancestor of the Janjua tribe of Punjab, who converted to Islam in the early decades of the 11th century during the reign of Mahmood of Ghazna. The centuries-old Malot Temple, built of red sandstone, stands on a hilltop in the Salt Range. The temple was recently conserved by the Archaeology Department though bushes can still be seen growing from its upper structure. The temple in Malot village holds a unique position among the temples of the Salt Range because of its imposing gateway, which was probably constructed at a later date. At present, there is no passage connecting the two structures. The floor levels of both structures are considerably higher than the present ground level of the surrounding area. However, clear evidence indicates that a built-up passage once connected them, approximately 2.4 metres above the current ground level. The distance between the temple and its gateway is 17.4 metres. A crudely built canopy on top of the temple is a much later addition, most probably constructed to serve as a watchtower. Although the exact dates of construction of the Malot Temple and its gateway are unknown, their Kashmiri architectural style places them between the 7th and 10th centuries of the Christian era, when the Salt Range was dominated by Kashmiri Hindu-Shahi dynasties. Both the temple and gateway are protected under the Antiquities Act, 1975. A close-up view of the intricate carvings on the wall of Malot Temple, showcasing the craftsmanship of its builders. The temple was recently conserved by the Archaeology Department. The Directorate of Archaeology, Punjab, launched a conservation and preservation project at Malot in 2021. The project was completed in 2023 at a cost of Rs12 million. The temple was conserved and restored, while wild plants and weeds were also removed from the site. However, in the absence of a caretaker, the weeds gradually returned. Another project for the beautification and development of Malot Fort is being undertaken by the TDCP. On Oct 1, the corporation posted a video on its official Facebook page, stating, “Discover the historic beauty of Malot Temple, Chakwal, where ancient architecture, rich heritage, and breathtaking landscapes come together to tell stories of the past. Explore the magnificent heritage of Punjab with TDCP.” Featuring a picture of Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz Sharif in its upper-right corner, the video showcased the fort’s scenic beauty and highlighted the development work being carried out at the site. The imposing gateway of Malot Temple which holds a unique position among the temples of the Salt Range. — Photos by the Writer The Punjab Tourism for Economic Growth Project (PTEGP) is a flagship initiative of the Punjab government, undertaken in collaboration with the World Bank, to transform tourism into a major driver of regional development, employment generation and revenue growth. An official, requesting anonymity, told Dawn that Malot Fort was also included in the PTEGP. “The funding was hefty, but it has not translated into work on the ground. This aspect needs to be investigated to establish where the money was spent, as the fort still presents a picture of neglect,” the official said. When approached, TDCP Regional Manager Mohammad Abbas Ashraf told Dawn that 80pc of the development work at Malot had been completed. “The work has been stopped due to a shortage of funds, but it will be completed soon,” he said. However, he did not disclose the exact cost of the ongoing TDCP project, which remains stalled. Sub-Divisional Officer Archaeology Aamir Shahzad told Dawn that his department had completed its project in 2023. “The fort needs a caretaker for its upkeep, but unfortunately, we are short of staff,” he said, adding that efforts were under way to hire security guards to look after the monument. Published in Dawn, November 16th, 2026

items.title: Ghana’s difficult reforms are bearing fruit – IMF
items.description: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) says Ghana is reaping the benefits of difficult policy reforms, with stronger-than-expected growth, single-digit inflation and an improved fiscal position. Speaking at a news conference in Washington, DC, IMF Director of Communications Julie Kozack said decisions taken under challenging circumstances were now supporting economic stability. “We’ve also seen a willingness by the authorities to undertake some very difficult policy decisions,” she said. Kozack noted that Ghana implemented its previous IMF-supported programme during a difficult period. However, the authorities’ decisions were now delivering results. “Those are now bearing fruit, as I said, in terms of stability and the strength of the economy.” She also highlighted public engagement as an important part of the reform process. “One thing we also saw in Ghana was an extensive social dialogue in the country, a lot of engagement with key stakeholders beyond the government to explain reforms, to get feedback, to understand broader priorities for the country,” she said. On economic performance, Kozack said growth had exceeded expectations. The economy expanded by 6% last year, while the Fund projects 5.7% growth this year. She said Ghana’s external position had strengthened, its debt-to-GDP ratio was around 50%, and inflation had fallen to single digits. According to her, Ghana achieved these gains despite global economic shocks, including pressure from energy prices. “The fiscal position in Ghana is now strong, and the primary surplus is on track to meet the year-end targets,” she said. Engagement with Ghana Kozack said the Fund’s engagement with Ghana was moving beyond crisis management as macroeconomic stability became more firmly established. Her comments also addressed Ghana’s decision to pursue a Policy Coordination Instrument. She said the focus was shifting “from crisis response, which was really the focus of the previous program, to supporting a consolidation of reforms and the building of longer-term resilience in the country”. Outlook for Ghana Looking ahead, Kozack said Ghana’s experience offered encouragement after years of economic difficulty. “Even a few years ago, I think the mood in Ghana was more difficult. It was a hard time for the country; it was a hard time for the people.” She said the next priority was to reinforce the economy’s ability to withstand future shocks. “The focus is really on strengthening and bolstering that resilience that comes next for the country.”

items.title: China-developed 10-ton e-aircraft completes first piloted flight
items.description: SHANGHAI: China’s independently developed 10-ton electric commercial aircraft CE-25A completed its maiden piloted flight on Saturday, according to the Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China (COMAC). The aircraft carried two pilots and one flight-test engineer during the flight in Binzhou, East China’s Shandong province. The aircraft operated normally, and all performance indicators met expectations, COMAC said. The CE-25A is COMAC’s first electric commercial aircraft. Designed mainly for intercity commercial flights, it can carry 19 passengers and has a maximum takeoff weight of 10 metric tons. It has a cruising speed of 300 km per hour, a cruising altitude of 2,400 metres and a range of 400 km. The aircraft completed its first unmanned autonomous flight on Feb 2 this year. Developed jointly by COMAC, Chinese battery maker CATL, Shanghai Jiao Tong University and other partners, the CE-25A has completed 19 unmanned autonomous flight validations. Instead of conventional turbofan or turboprop engines, the CE-25A uses a distributed electric propulsion system consisting of 10 electric ducted fans mounted along the top of its wings. This layout aims to reduce noise and enable takeoffs and landings on shorter runways. The Civil Aviation Administration of China (CAAC) has formally accepted COMAC’s type certificate application under transport-category regulations, initiating the inspection process required before commercial passenger service can begin. items.title: US officials say violence against Christians in Nigeria remains a key concern
items.description: Violence against Nigerian Christians remains a key concern, the US State Department said, a year after the Trump administration accused Nigeria of violating religious freedoms and designated ​it as a “country of particular concern” (CPC). President Donald Trump last November threatened military action ‌against the West African nation over the treatment of Christians. The Nigerian government rejected the CPC designation, saying it was based on misinformation and faulty data. The Reuters Daily Briefing newsletter provides all the news you need to start your day. Sign up here. Assistant Secretary of State Frank Garcia, speaking to ​a panel in Congress on Thursday, said the State Department was treating the ​issue as a top priority, working closely with Nigerian authorities to address ⁠the violence waged against Christian communities and hold those responsible to account. “Unfortunately, the violence ​has not stopped,” Garcia said. Nigeria’s Information Minister Mohammed Idris did not immediately respond to a ​request for comment. Nigerian leaders have previously said the country is dealing with terrorism, not persecution of Christians, and that they would welcome US help in fighting Islamist insurgents as long as the country’s ​territorial integrity is respected. NIGERIAN ELECTIONS LOOM Insecurity tops the list of campaign issues ahead of ​Nigeria’s presidential and parliamentary elections, set for January 16, 2027. Africa’s most populous nation is battling an ‌Islamist insurgency, ⁠banditry and farmer-herder clashes in its northern regions as well as kidnapping for ransom in the south. US Assistant Secretary of State Riley Barnes said Nigeria had hired police, deployed forest guards and increased prosecutions and arrests following the US designation, but these moves had ​not led to greater ​safety for Christians ⁠in the country’s Middle Belt region. Citing also a sharp increase in violence against Christians in Nigeria’s central Plateau State, US Representative Riley Moore, ​a West Virginia Republican, asked: “What is the (State) Department doing to make ​sure the ⁠Nigerian government brings the fight to the militias where Christians are dying? And before you answer that, we cannot take this CPC designation off this country. They have not done enough.” Nigeria, ⁠home ​to more than 200 ethnic groups practising Christianity, Islam ​and traditional faiths, has a history of coexistence but has also seen sporadic violence, often driven by ethnic tensions ​and competition over scarce resources.

items.title: ‘How Tinubu will end insecurity ready’
items.description: By Dapo Akinrefon ABUJA — THE All Progressives Congress APC, Presidential Campaign Council, APC-PCC, yesterday, unveiled President Bola Tinubu defence plan to end the 17-year scourge of insecurity ravaging parts of Nigeria through a comprehensive five-year strategic defence operations plan. Read Also: Igini to Trump: Tie Nigeria-US relations to credible polls The APC-PCC said the plan is designed to strengthen the country’s security architecture, improve military effectiveness, and ensure a coordinated response to emerging threats. Spokesperson of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, Dele Alake, who disclosed this in a statement, said the plan provided a long-term framework for aligning defence priorities, operational requirements, capability development, and expenditure with Nigeria’s current and anticipated security challenges. He also said ongoing military operations across the country had led to the elimination of more than 15,000 Boko Haram terrorists and bandits, with more than 130,000 fighters and dependants of Boko Haram surrendering through Operation Safe Corridor. Alaka said: “The initiative is a major component of President Tinubu’s determination to reposition the nation’s security architecture toward a more coordinated, intelligence-led, technology-enabled, and prevention-oriented system capable of addressing terrorism, banditry, kidnapping, and other forms of criminality. “In the last three years, the scale of the administration’s ongoing military operations across the country has led to the elimination of more than 15,000 Boko Haram terrorists and bandits, with more than 130,000 fighters and dependants of Boko Haram having surrendered through Operation Safe Corridor, the Federal Government’s rehabilitation programme for repentant insurgents. “The figures underscore the administration’s two-phase approach of sustained military operations and non-kinetic interventions to address insecurity.” On the expansion of military formations, manpower, he said the plan would “strengthen the Nigerian Army’s operational capacity and improve responses to security threats.” According to him, President Tinubu has created four new Army divisions and restructured existing military formations. He added: “The reforms aim to expand operational coverage, decentralise military operations, and enable troops to respond more swiftly to security threats across the country. “The President has also approved the establishment of two additional Army depots in Osogbo, Osun State, and in Amasiri-Edda, Ebonyi State, to expand military training capacity and accelerate the recruitment and training of new soldiers. “Each depot can accommodate 6,000 recruits at a time, bringing their combined training capacity to 12,000 soldiers. “The Osogbo facility’s capacity is already being demonstrated, with 5,210 recruits currently undergoing training there. “The expansion of training facilities is expected to reduce recruit turnaround time and increase the number of soldiers available for deployment. “To further the manpower expansion drive, President Tinubu also approved recruiting an additional 28,000 soldiers to strengthen the military’s presence on the ground and enhance its operational effectiveness. “The President also approved recruiting 50,000 additional police officers as part of broader efforts to reinforce internal security, improve policing capacity, and strengthen the country’s response to criminal activities. “Beyond investments in equipment, technology and training, the administration is also investing in military accommodation and operational infrastructure to improve personnel welfare and effectiveness. “One such project is the 700-unit military barracks in Ikere-Ekiti, Ekiti State, designed to provide military personnel with a professional living and working environment and essential military infrastructure. “The facilities are expected to provide the accommodation and operational support personnel need while strengthening the military’s capacity to maintain an effective presence in the area. “These measures reflect the administration’s determination to address manpower and infrastructure gaps, improve the capacity of security agencies, and ensure personnel are adequately trained, equipped, and deployed to areas facing security challenges”, Alake said. On intelligence, surveillance and coordination, the APC-PCC spokesperson said: “Under the Five-Year Strategic Defence Operations Plan, the federal government is adopting a more strategic approach to national defence by ensuring that investments in the security sector are guided by clearly identified threats, operational requirements and national priorities. “The plan is expected to strengthen combat readiness, address critical capability gaps, optimise available resources and minimise unnecessary expenditure and wastage.” Vanguard News The post ‘How Tinubu will end insecurity ready’ appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Igini to Trump: Tie Nigeria-US relations to credible polls
items.description: A former Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, Resident Electoral Commissioner, Mike Igini, has urged US President, Donald Trump, to link America’s immigration policy and diplomatic relations with Nigeria to credible conduct of the country’s 2027 general elections. Read Also: ‘How Tinubu will end insecurity ready’ Igini said electoral malpractice, corruption, insecurity and poor governance were among the factors forcing Nigerians to seek opportunities abroad, arguing that credible elections and accountable leadership could help address the root causes of migration. In an open letter dated November 13, 2026, and addressed to Trump at the White House, the former REC proposed a policy he called the “No Mandate Fraud” Doctrine, urging the US to combine preventive diplomacy, independent election monitoring and targeted sanctions against individuals involved in electoral violations. He argued that border enforcement alone could not address migration without tackling the governance failures driving Nigerians out of their country. “Nigerians are not leaving Nigeria because they do not love their country. They are leaving because of decades of persistent electoral malpractice, corruption, insecurity and weak public accountability that have undermined Nigerians’ confidence in government,” he wrote. Igini urged Trump to send a high-level delegation to engage President Bola Tinubu, political parties, presidential and governorship candidates, INEC and other relevant institutions ahead of the elections. He said the delegation should communicate Washington’s position that credible elections, peaceful political competition and respect for constitutional rights were central to US interests in Nigeria. He also proposed visa restrictions, financial sanctions and asset freezes, where legally justified, against electoral officials found culpable of manipulating results, falsifying records or committing other electoral offences. The former REC extended the call for accountability to judicial officers whose misconduct in electoral cases was established by credible evidence, as well as security personnel involved in voter intimidation, electoral violence and suppression of opposition parties. He identified the police, Department of State Services, Armed Forces and Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps as institutions expected to protect voters and ensure impartial enforcement of the law. Igini further urged the US to support credible domestic and international election observers to monitor the process before, during and after the polls, particularly voter intimidation, security neutrality, polling-unit results and transparent collation. Explaining the benefits to Washington, he said credible elections could reduce migration pressure, strengthen security cooperation and create opportunities for stronger economic relations. He also identified potential US investment in Nigeria’s energy sector, particularly electricity development, through technology transfer and private-sector partnerships. Warning against waiting for an electoral crisis before intervening, Igini said: “The time to act is before the election, not after a crisis has occurred.” He urged Washington to make clear that it would not conduct business as usual with any government produced through electoral fraud, stressing that sanctions must be lawful and supported by credible evidence. items.title: Riesgo de involución
items.description: Desde que Vox consiguió en 2019 por primera vez representación en el Congreso, con 2,6 millones de votos, la política española se ha visto abocada a tomar posición ante la posibilidad de que un día pudiera llegar a gobernar. Esa posibilidad se hizo realidad en 2023, cuando el PP aceptó integrarlo en coalición en los gobiernos de cinco comunidades autónomas — ahora reducidas a cuatro: Extremadura, Aragón, Castilla y León y Andalucía—. Si hoy Alberto Núñez Feijóo no es presidente del Gobierno, es en buena parte por la reacción a aquellos pactos. En las elecciones del 29-N, las encuestas pronostican una mayoría absoluta holgada del tándem PP y Vox, que no disimulan su vocación de coalición hasta el punto de coordinar sus candidaturas al Senado . Si ocurre, será la primera vez que la extrema derecha entre en el Gobierno de España desde el franquismo. Ningún análisis político puede obviar ese escenario. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Euskadi pone a prueba el crecimiento de Bildu
items.description: El 29-N se juega en Euskadi en un tablero doble: el nacional y el vasco. Las dos principales fuerzas políticas vascas marcan tendencias contrapuestas ante esta cita. EH Bildu parece no tener techo y, en cambio, el PNV mira con preocupación dónde puede estar su suelo electoral. Todas las prospecciones coinciden en que un partido crece y el otro se desinfla . La consecuencia que podría darse es que, por primera vez, la izquierda abertzale sea la fuerza más votada en unas elecciones generales. Es un aviso a navegantes de cara a las elecciones municipales y forales de mayo de 2027 y a las autonómicas de 2028. EH Bildu corre con el viento a favor para reforzar su aspiración de ser alternativa de gobierno en Ajuria Enea; el PNV trata de minimizar daños y sostener la supremacía en la comunidad. PSE-EE y PP pelean por electores que en otros comicios optan por marcas nacionalistas y ahora eligen su papeleta guiados por el dilema Sánchez-Feijóo. Seguir leyendo

A 25.902 millones de kilómetros de nuestro mundo, la mayor distancia a la que ha llegado ningún otro objeto fabricado por el ser humano. items.title: Simulacros, huellas, planos y zapatillas: siete expediciones a Montserrat para aclarar la muerte de Isak Andic
items.description: El camino de tierra por el que transitó Isak Andic al morir, el 14 de diciembre de 2024, ya no es el mismo. El punto donde cayó —un sendero de metro y medio de ancho, seguido de una rampa inclinada y un acantilado— ha mutado. Y eso, que vale para tantos caminos, pasa de manera más acentuada en la montaña de Montserrat, un macizo que sufre constantes desprendimientos de rocas y que se erosiona con el paso del tiempo. El lugar en el que perdió la vida, a los 71 años, el fundador de Mango , también ha cambiado por la acción humana: excursionistas habituales y curiosos pero, sobre todo, los agentes de los Mossos d’Esquadra especializados en la montaña que, hasta en siete ocasiones, han explorado palmo a palmo el Camí de les Feixades, en busca de que el terreno arrojara luz sobre lo que ocurrió. items.title: Leonor Watling: “Soy afortunada, vivo en una casa que comparto con el banco”
items.description: Leonor Watling (Madrid, 51 años) lleva más de tres décadas trabajando frente a las cámaras. Por eso, cuando le propusieron protagonizar una ficción sonora, no lo dudó. “No tenía que llevar maquillaje ni vestuario. Me pareció un sueño”, reconoce la actriz y cantante. “Los actores trabajamos con nuestra imagen, así que siempre estamos sometidos a la presión estética. Antes era muy difícil explicar esa ansiedad asociada a la fama. Ahora, con las redes sociales, es más fácil. Ahora, cualquiera con una cuenta de Instagram sabe de lo que hablo”. Watling protagoniza con Alberto San Juan y Alejandro García la segunda temporada de Simulacro , la exitosa producción de audio del guionista Julio Rojas [creador de Caso 63 , la ficción sonora hispanohablante más escuchada del siglo XXI] que reflexiona sobre temas como la inteligencia artificial y las difusas líneas entre realidad y ficción y verdad y mentira. El campo de la gran batalla de esta COP31 será el texto final con el que la presidencia de la conferencia, que ostenta Turquía en colaboración con Australia, quiere que se cierre una cita que se celebra mientras suenan las alarmas por la aceleración del cambio climático, al que ahora se le suma el fenómeno de El Niño . Ese texto ( cover decision , en inglés), que no siempre se aprueba en las COP, suele tener una importante carga política y sirve de termómetro para calibrar el vigor de la lucha internacional contra el cambio climático, que no atraviesa su mejor momento ahora . items.title: Un parking, un viaje a Portugal y los cordones de un zapato: la investigación que dio con los ‘topos’ del CNI
items.description: El día que la Policía entró en la vivienda del agente 7691 (58 años, Galicia) encontró en la nevera un imán con la imagen de Vladimir Putin en el que se leía: Long live Putin! ( ¡Larga vida a Putin! ). La casa que registraron está a seis minutos en coche del Centro Nacional de Inteligencia (CNI), donde él trabajaba como jefe del área de Rusia, y allí encontraron también 1.450 euros en una caja fuerte portátil y un wallet (monedero) de criptomonedas. Ese 29 de septiembre de 2023, cuando no solo él fue arrestado, sino también uno de sus compañeros dentro del CNI, poco podía imaginar lo que estaba ocurriendo. Un equipo del Centro llevaba meses siguiendo al milímetro sus pasos con la suficiente distancia para no ser detectados. Habían colocado una cámara camuflada en su despacho dentro del edificio que vela por la seguridad nacional. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Oil prices fall on expectations of coming supply surplus
items.description: Oil prices fell on Monday on expectations of a supply surplus as shipments from the Middle East through the Strait of Hormuz have nearly returned to pre-war levels and the US took steps to support the movement of fuel cargoes between domestic ports. Brent futures were down 47 cents, or 0.49%, to $95.37 a barrel by 0145 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude fell 23 ​cents, or 0.26%, to $88.33. Oil closed lower on Friday as the market weighed signs of lowering geopolitical risk ​from the US-Israeli war against Iran, now in its ninth month. The benchmarks fell 16% and 13% the prior week, respectively. The International Energy Agency said on Friday that the world oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of this ​year, as Middle East exports recover faster than global oil demand despite continued attacks on shipping. “For the first time since the US-Iran conflict began, traders are actively contemplating the possibility of excess supply rather than persistent tightness. That shift in narrative is clearly dampening the tone,” said Tim Waterer, chief analyst at KCM Trade. Oil supply will average 105 ​million barrels per day in the fourth quarter, 1.7 million bpd higher than forecast demand, the IEA said. The ​IEA had previously forecast a fourth-quarter supply deficit. The agency also gave more details of remaining volumes to come from a record release ‌of ⁠oil from its members’ emergency reserves pledged in March, saying 71 million barrels would be made available by the end of February including 15 million barrels of diesel to ease market tightness. Prices were also pressured down by the US decision to extend a waiver of a shipping law that will continue to allow foreign-flagged ships to transport oil and fuels such as gasoline and diesel more easily between US ports. US President Donald Trump extended for 90 days a waiver of the Jones Act, which requires US-flagged ships to carry cargo between US ports, a White House official said on ​Friday. Waiving the rule increases the number of tankers available to carry commodities between US ports. Still, ⁠Waterer noted that while supply was loosening, shipping rates remained high, putting a floor on oil prices. Rates remain high because of the risks tankers face carrying crude through the Strait of Hormuz, and because fewer ships are shuttling oil through the waterway for transfer to other ships that take shipments to refineries. On Sunday night, Iran’s navy said that an oil tanker caught fire after striking a naval mine east of ​the Strait of Hormuz, state media reported. Reuters could not independently verify the report.

items.title: How identity politics is redrawing the India-Bangladesh borderlands
items.description: THE India–Bangladesh borderlands are not simply spaces of territorial contestation. They are landscapes shaped by shared histories, cultural continuities and deeply intertwined human relationships. These borderlands hold a profound place in Bangladesh’s history. At Baidyanathtala (later renamed Mujibnagar), near the Indian border, the country’s first government took its oath on April 17, 1971. For decades, despite political tensions and an increasingly securitised border, communities on both sides maintained relationships through cross-border marriages, religious practices, trade, shared languages and everyday interactions. The political meaning of these borderlands extends beyond territorial security and migration management, raising a more fundamental question: who has the legitimate right to belong? Recent developments in India’s northeastern border states point towards an increasingly troubling politics of identity. Demolition drives in Assam’s Dhubri district targeting villages largely inhabited by Bengali-speaking Assamese Muslims, the normalisation of derogatory expressions such as Miya, and controversies surrounding villagers’ encounters with the Indian Border Security Force in Tripura have raised questions that extend beyond individual incidents. Who is considered an Indian? Why are certain communities repeatedly required to prove their legitimacy? These questions reveal a changing relationship between territory, identity and citizenship. For people living along the border, belonging is increasingly negotiated through markers that extend beyond legal documentation: their names, language, attire, religious practices and perceived cultural affiliations. The border, in this sense, is becoming more than a geographical boundary. It is also a political instrument for distinguishing between those who are considered insiders and those who are treated as outsiders. This is the cartography of othering: the process through which political narratives redraw the social boundaries of belonging, even within internationally recognised national territories. The problem becomes particularly acute when religious identity is conflated with national allegiance. Bengali-speaking Muslims in West Bengal, Assam and Tripura are frequently situated within political narratives of illegal migration and demographic insecurity. Migration and citizenship are legitimate matters of public policy. States have the authority to regulate their borders and establish legal procedures. But when an entire community is persistently viewed through the lens of suspicion, the distinction between immigration enforcement and identity-based exclusion becomes increasingly difficult to maintain. The political influence of the Bharatiya Janata Party in India’s border states has also contributed to a changing political vocabulary around migration, nationalism and religious identity. Polarising and hateful statements by political leaders, particularly those associated with the political leadership of Assam and West Bengal, have contributed to the normalisation of exclusionary narratives, gradually shifting the boundaries of what is considered acceptable in public discourse. The territorial imagination underlying some political statements is eq­­u­­ally significant. References by Ind­­ian politicians to Chittagong, Noak­hali and Sylhet as territories that should have belonged to India, or as historical mistakes associated with Partition, are not simply rhetorical provocations. They invoke an unfinished geographical imagination in which historical grievance, religious majoritarianism and territorial nati­o­­n­­alism intersect. Such narratives deserve scrutiny not because every political statement signals an immediate territorial ambition, but beca­use they can reshape how neighbouring societies perceive one another. The consequences of this politics do not stop at the border fence. For Bangladesh, these developments carry both political and social implications. Social media has become an important arena where statements and incidents from India’s border states are circulated, interpreted and sometimes amplified without sufficient context. Reports of discrimination or violence can generate legitimate concern, but misinformation and emotionally charged responses can also deepen antagonism within Bangladesh. The result is a transnational politics of suspicion in which developments on one side of the border influence perceptions and political narratives on the other. In this context, Myanmar’s Rohin­gya crisis offers a crucial warning. The progressive exclusion of the Roh­i­­n­­gya from citizenship, their institutionalised marginalisation and eventual mass displacement demonstrate how the gradual denial of belonging can develop into a profound humanitarian catastrophe. Bangladesh continues to bear the consequences nea­rly a decade after the mass exodus of 2017. India and Myanmar are fundamentally different political contexts. The comparison, therefore, should not suggest an inevitable repetition of the Rohingya experience. History, however, offers an important lesson: major crises rarely emerge overnight. They can begin with the normalisation of suspicion, the politicisation of identity and the gradual erosion of a community’s social and legal legitimacy. Published in Dawn, November 16th, 2026

items.title: Cinq pays européens vont envoyer des migrants au Rwanda
items.description: Cinq pays de l'UE, dont l'Allemagne et le Danemark, vont annoncer lundi la signature d'un accord avec le Rwanda pour créer les premiers centres pour migrants expulsés d'Europe. Ce projet de « hubs de retour », qui fait bondir les défenseurs des droits humains, va être dévoilé lors d'une conférence de presse à Vienne, en milieu d'après-midi, ont indiqué des sources concordantes à l'AFP. Une initiative également pilotée par la Grèce, l'Autriche et les Pays-Bas, tous partisans d'une ligne migratoire très ferme. Voilà des mois que ces cinq pays européens planchent sur l'idée d'envoyer des personnes dont la demande d'asile aurait été refusée dans des centres en Afrique. De Munich à Bruxelles, en passant par Copenhague, un petit groupe de diplomates, ministres et fonctionnaires ont multiplié les réunions pour définir les contours de ces tout premiers « hubs ». Tout au long de leurs échanges, ils ont insisté pour garder le pays hôte secret, de crainte de compromettre les négociations. « Nous verrons la semaine prochaine à Vienne », s'est contenté de dire le chancelier autrichien Christian Stocker vendredi. Mais selon plusieurs diplomates et personnes proches des négociations s'exprimant auprès de l'AFP sous couvert d'anonymat, le nom du Rwanda ne fait plus le moindre doute. Une délégation rwandaise sera d'ailleurs présente lundi à Vienne pour participer à une conférence sur la migration. Inquiétude des ONG L'objectif affiché est d'ouvrir des premiers centres en 2027. Ces derniers ont été imaginés en lien avec la Commission européenne, il y a un an et demi, afin d'accroître significativement le nombre des expulsions de migrants du territoire européen. Le raisonnement de ces cinq pays est double: en plus d'expulser les déboutés d'asile, ils espèrent ainsi décourager des migrants de tenter de s'installer sur le continent européen. Ces « hubs de retour » sont toutefois très critiqués par la gauche et les ONG, qui s'inquiètent du traitement des migrants dans ces établissements. Le président Emmanuel Macron avait vivement critiqué le concept, jugeant que ces centres n'étaient « ni efficaces », ni conformes aux valeurs de l'UE. Le choix du Rwanda suscite également des inquiétudes. L'ONG Human Rights Watch pointe notamment du doigt les antécédents bien documentés du pays en matière de répression ou de détentions arbitraires. Quel sera le sort réservé aux personnes sur place ? Quelles contreparties le Rwanda va-t-il obtenir en échange de son accord ? Le projet ira-t-il de l'avant, en dépit des menaces de recours judiciaires? De nombreuses questions restent aussi en suspens. Afin de dissiper certaines d'entre elles, les cinq pays européens entendent d'abord lancer ce centre à une très petite échelle, a expliqué une source diplomatique à l'AFP. Une sorte de projet pilote. L'idée est d'y envoyer d'abord une vingtaine de déboutés d'asile par pays européen concerné, probablement des hommes majeurs, appréhendés à la frontière. Et d'anticiper tous les scénarios possibles: qui les transportera, que se passera-t-il si l'un des migrants tombe malade, etc… ? A en croire plusieurs sources proches des négociations, les établissements ne seront pas des centres de détention fermés. Le Rwanda souhaite les appeler des « centres d'accueil » et pourrait y proposer des formations professionnelles. L'Organisation internationale pour les migrations (OIM) pourrait prêter main forte sur place. Le projet raté du Royaume-Uni Ces cinq pays européens ne sont pas les premiers à s'intéresser au pays d'Afrique de l'Est quand il s'agit de migration. Le Royaume-Uni avait annoncé en 2022 son intention d'y ouvrir un centre pour demandeurs d'asile. Mais le projet avait finalement été abandonné par le gouvernement travailliste de Keir Starmer, en raison d'obstacles judiciaires. Jeudi, son successeur Andy Burnham a toutefois dit suivre « avec intérêt » la tentative des européens. Le Rwanda a également accepté d'accueillir des personnes expulsées des États-Unis sous la présidence de Donald Trump. Si le projet pilote est concluant, les cinq pays de l'UE envisagent également de l'élargir à d'autres, comme l'Ouganda et l'Ouzbékistan. The post Cinq pays européens vont envoyer des migrants au Rwanda appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Nearly 1,500 migrants arrive in Canary Islands in one day
items.description: Almost 1,500 migrants arrived in Spain’s Canary Islands on Saturday, the highest number in a single day since 2020, the EFE ​news agency reported on Sunday, citing the maritime rescue service. The Spanish coastguard rescued 1,488 people in 14 boats, EFE reported, continuing a surge of arrivals from West African countries to the Spanish archipelago since October. The previous one-day record was 1,461 people rescued in waters off the Canary Islands on November 7, 2020, maritime rescue services said on Sunday. While migrant arrivals have declined so far this year compared with the same period last year, last month’s sharp increase placed additional pressure on reception and emergency services on some of the Canary Islands, particularly the smaller, less densely populated ones. Authorities said one boat on Saturday carried 240 people, including 12 women and 36 children. Authorities took the rescued migrants to El Hierro, one of the smallest Canary Islands. Most of the ‌people ⁠were from Senegal, Gambia and Guinea-Bissau. Twelve boats arrived in El Hierro, plus one in Gran Canaria and another in Tenerife. Spain’s Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres will visit El Hierro on Sunday to discuss the ​surge in migrant arrivals. The ​Atlantic route ⁠from West Africa to the Canary Islands is one of the world’s deadliest migration crossings. Thousands of migrants attempt ​the journey each year in overcrowded boats, seeking to ​reach Spanish ⁠territory despite rough seas, strong currents and long distances. Arrivals tend to pick up in the autumn months, when sea conditions along the route are generally ⁠calmer ​and more favourable for crossings. Migrant arrivals to the ​Canary Islands between January and October 31 were down 5.5% from the same period last ​year, government data show.

items.title: Klopp says FIFA worse under Infantino than Blatter
items.description: FIFA president Gianni Infantino should be replaced, as he has made world football’s governing body worse than it was under disgraced former chief Sepp Blatter, Germany coach Jürgen Klopp said on Sunday. Speaking a day before Germany’s Nations League game against the Netherlands, Klopp said the situation at FIFA was potentially ​worse than under Blatter, who stepped down amid a ​corruption scandal and later faced criminal charges. “The opinion is ⁠unanimous that a change would make sense,” Klopp told ​a press conference. “I didn’t think things could get worse after Sepp ​Blatter, but someone managed to do just that.” Infantino, also Swiss, was elected FIFA president in 2016 after a corruption scandal brought Blatter’s tenure to ​an end. Blatter was later acquitted in a Swiss ​criminal case concerning a two-million-Swiss-franc payment to former UEFA president Michel Platini. “At the ‌moment ⁠we think that if Infantino goes that then the next one could maybe do it better. I think it is possible to make it better,” Klopp said. “There are certainly people ​out there who ​care about ⁠the future of football and have no financial interest linked to that, and if they come ​together and one of them would become ​president, it ⁠would be helpful.” Infantino, who is up for re-election in March 2027 and who has vowed to stay on , came under heavy criticism ⁠in ​July after an unsuccessful attempt to bring ​private investors into a new FIFA commercial entity holding rights linked to competitions, ​including the World Cup.

items.title: Salah breaks Egypt scoring record as Tunisia lose to Libya
items.description: Tunisia’s dismal ​run continued with a 2-0 home defeat by Libya in an Africa Cup of Nations qualifier on ‌Friday, while Mohamed Salah became Egypt’s record scorer in their 5-0 rout of Malawi. Cape Verde and Nigeria secured key wins after disappointing starts to the 2027 qualifying campaign, while past winners South Africa and Zambia drew frustrating home matches. Salah ​scored twice late on to take his international tally to 70 and surpass former captain Hossam Hassan’s record. ​New coach Ali Maher began his tenure with a comprehensive victory in Cairo that put Egypt ⁠top of Group B. Tunisia were the only one of Africa’s 10 teams at this year’s World Cup to exit ​following the group stage, and they fired coach Sabri Lamouchi after their opening defeat. Their woes continued against neighbours Libya on ​Friday as they lost 2-0 in Sfax to a penalty from Ali Youssef on the stroke of halftime and a 62nd-minute effort from Hamdou El Houni. The defeat left Tunisia with two points at the halfway stage of their Group H campaign and in danger of missing ​next year’s finals, which would end their record run of 17 successive appearances. Coach Mouin Chaabani’s short reign is ​also under threat. Cape Verde, who thrilled the neutrals with their run to the second round at the World Cup, had lost their opening ‌qualifiers ⁠in September but were back to winning ways on Friday with a 4-2 home triumph over Liberia, with debutant Derensili Sanches Fernandes from Huddersfield Town among the scorers. Nigeria made multiple changes to their line-up after a 3-0 loss to Guinea Bissau in their last outing two months ago and bounced back with giant striker Tolu Arokodare scoring twice in their 3-1 ​win over Tanzania. CAME FROM BEHIND Defender ​Jean Girumugisha scored seven minutes ⁠from time for tiny Burundi to draw 1-1 away at Zambia in Group I while Ryan Ogam’s 90th minute strike saw Kenya hold South Africa 2-2 in Johannesburg in Group ​D. Mali came from behind to beat Rwanda 3-2 in Bamako and win a third ​match in Group ⁠K and move within one win of a place in the finals. Mamadou Camara snatched their late winner. African Footballer of the Year Achraf Hakimi scored twice as Morocco beat Niger 5-1 in Casablanca to maintain their perfect start in Group A and move ⁠closer ​to qualification. There are three more matches on Saturday to complete the third ​round of the group qualifiers which marks the halfway mark of the campaign. The fourth round of group fixtures is on Monday and Tuesday and the ​last two rounds in March. The 2027 finals are to be co-hosted by Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda from June 19-July 17.

items.title: Nigeria cautions against travel via Ethiopia’s main airport due to altitude
items.description: Nigeria’s government has cautioned its citizens, especially those with medical conditions, against travelling via Ethiopia’s main airport because of its altitude. The foreign ministry in Abuja said 16 Nigerians with underlying health problems had died this year while transiting through Addis Ababa. The city sits at an altitude of 2,334m (7,657ft) above sea level, making it one of the world’s highest capitals. Bole International Airport is a major hub for travel between Africa, the Middle East and Asia, serving millions of passengers a year. Nigeria said those with cardiovascular and respiratory conditions were at an increased risk. The Nigerian foreign ministry did not disclose the identities of the travellers it said had died, nor the cause of death. It urged anyone with a health condition exacerbated by high altitudes to “exercise caution” when planning a journey via Addis Ababa and “obtain appropriate medical guidance” before doing so. The ministry stressed that it did not want to discourage Nigerians from travelling through the Ethiopian capital. Visiting an area at a high altitude can be dangerous for people with heart and lung diseases, as the air is thinner and so less oxygen can get into the bloodstream, experts say. This means the heart has to work harder to get enough oxygen to different parts of the body, which can sometimes lead to heart failure among those with existing conditions, according to the American Heart Association. The lack of oxygen at high altitudes can cause adverse effects such as dizziness, fatigue and shortness of breath among healthy people – which can cause complications for people with lung disease, studies show.

items.title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia’s ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
items.description: Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia’s former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says. Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees. Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business. Megaspeed said it was aware of reports “containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence”. It added that it “conducts legitimate and lawful business” and has “retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation”. But while Alice Huang is said to have stepped down from her role as Megaspeed director near the end of 2023, there were suspicions that she was still heavily involved in the firm’s operations, according to Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS C4ADS said that Huang was still “practically in control” of Megaspeed even after she had handed over the reins of the firm. Huang – who is of no relation to Nvidia’s former boss – had been investigated by Singapore authorities in February 2025 as part of the country’s probe into Megaspeed and other companies. Also on Sunday, US Congressman John Moolenaar said that Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Select Committee on China, which he chairs, as well as the House Foreign Affairs and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. The committee heads had threatened to issue subpoenas to Huang if he did not comply with their requests to testify. Moolenaar told CBS, BBC’s US partner, that none were ultimately issued. Huang’s testimony is expected to take place behind close doors, with the dates still being finalised. “That’s going to be a very important meeting to understand to what degree privileged information was accessed, and to what degree this potential alleged Chinese spy influenced Nvidia’s philosophy and may have had an influence on some of our policies with respect to AI and export controls,” the congressman told the Face The Nation programme. Separately, a group of tech leaders, including Space X’s Elon Musk, have been trying to rally support to have Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO. A representative for Huang declined to comment on a Financial Times Sunday report suggesting he was discussing a comeback to the firm he co-founded. The BBC understands that Huang’s chances of returning to lead Nvidia are very low while the company’s internal investigations are ongoing. The move would also face scrutiny from Washington, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling for Nvidia to hire its next CEO from outside the company. On Friday, Bessent had blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick’s Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips. Bessent told CNBC that several agencies “were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months… but Commerce has the pen… and you will have to ask them about their internal process”. The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals. Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department’s role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips. Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced semiconductors to China. Singapore does not prohibit transferring advanced AI chips to companies abroad, but such moves can breach US export controls. Singapore has said that while it does not enforce “unilateral export controls imposed by other countries” it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations. Megaspeed said it “designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes”. It said this includes “US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate”. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a “pretext for imposing a technological blockade” on AI technology.
