items.title: Punjab sugar millers snub order to begin crushing from weekend
items.description: • Only Ramzan Sugar Mills complies with provincial directive • Millers, farmers expected to hold pressers today • Growers demand immediate support price, seek PM’s intervention LAHORE: Most sugar mills across Punjab failed to begin sugarcane crushing on Sunday, defying a provincial government directive that mandated operations start by Nov 15. Only Ramzan Sugar Mills complied with the order issued by the Punjab Food Safety and Consumer Protection Department on behalf of the governor, according to an official of the Pakistan Sugar Mills Association (PSMA). The notification directed mill operators to purchase the crop and start the cane crushing season within 24 hours, while instructing deputy commissioners to ensure compliance, with copies sent to the federal secretaries for national food security and industries. Both the PSMA north zone and farmer groups have scheduled press conferences for Monday (today) to address the standoff. Khalid Hussain Bath, president of a farmers’ group, said the government’s notification proved ineffective, with mills remaining closed in Punjab and crushing yet to begin in Sindh. He said the delay was causing financial losses to growers already facing market uncertainty and higher prices for di-ammonium phosphate (DAP) fertiliser. Bath demanded that the government immediately announce a sugarcane support price, ensure mills purchase all approved crop varieties and provide surplus sugar to farmers. He also urged Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to take immediate notice of their grievances. According to official sources, mills will determine sugarcane prices under a market-based mechanism while the provincial government monitors rates to safeguard growers’ interests. Sugarcane has been cultivated over 2.452 million acres in Punjab this year, 16pc higher than last year’s area, the sources said. Earlier this month, Minister for National Food Security and Research Rana Tanveer Hussain said that the Sugar Advisory Board had set Nov 15 for the nationwide start of the crushing season. The decision followed extensive consultations with provincial governments, the PSMA, cane commissioners and representatives from the ministries of industries, production and commerce to prevent delays that could disadvantage growers. Chairing the meeting, attended by a PSMA delegation led by Chaudhry Zaka Ashraf, the minister warned of strict action against any mill failing to start operations on time. “Payment of dues to farmers will be ensured before the commencement of crushing,” he said. “The government is making all decisions in the best interest of farmers to prevent their exploitation.” Published in Dawn, November 16th, 2026

items.title: CDA finalises revised PC-I for Islamabad cricket stadium at Rs16.7bn
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The Capital Development Authority (CDA) has finalised the modified PC-I of the Islamabad Cricket Stadium, increasing the estimated cost of the project from Rs11.9 billion to Rs16.7bn for both packages, covering the grey structure, finishing and electrical works. “Modified PC-Is for both phases have been completed and will soon be presented before the upcoming CDA Development Working Party (DWP) for approval,” a CDA officer told Dawn. He said the cost of the project, which was previously estimated at Rs11.9bn in an unapproved PC-I, had increased to Rs16.7bn after the inclusion of additional components. These included the grey structure, finishing, lighting, heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems, preparation of the ground and pitches, and a security camera system. The officer said the earlier PC-I envisaged a seating capacity of 25,000. However, when the CDA invited requests for proposals earlier this year, it was decided to increase the capacity. Several other components had also been added to the modified PC-I, he added. Stadium to be developed in two phases; CDA aims to complete entire project within a year Asked about the delay in the groundbreaking, the officer said the modification of the PC-I had nothing to do with the commencement of construction. “The bidding process for the grey structure and road network has already been completed, and groundbreaking of Phase-I (grey structure) will be held soon. It will be completed within six months,” he said. Another CDA officer said that after approval of the PC-I, the authority would initiate the tendering process for Phase-II as well. “We will try to complete both phases, covering the entire project, within one year,” he said. Recently, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi had announced in a press talk that the groundbreaking of the stadium would take place within 10 days. A Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) official indicated that Pakistan was likely to host some matches of the ICC Women’s T20 World Cup 2028 at the proposed Islamabad stadium. “If the Islamabad stadium project is completed on time, we will organise some matches of the Women’s World Cup in 2028 in the capital,” the official said. According to the CDA, the stadium will have a seating capacity of 35,000, making it the largest cricket stadium in Pakistan. It will be a replica of the Dubai Cricket Stadium, the official said. The CDA is constructing the stadium at the foothills of the Margalla Hills near Sector D-12. Some months ago, the authority received a bid of Rs8.9bn from a joint venture of Habib-ZKB-EA. Of the total amount, Rs5.8bn was allocated for the three-tier stadium structure and Rs3.1bn for external works, including three kilometres of three-plus-three-lane roads and associated infrastructure. Later, the CDA secured a rebate of Rs400 million from the construction firm, bringing the contract amount down to Rs8.5bn. It is relevant to note that the site selected for the stadium falls in Zone III, where construction activity is generally banned and local landowners are not allowed to build houses on their land. However, the CDA maintains that sports and recreational activities are permissible in the zone and that the construction of a cricket stadium falls within the permitted activities. In the past, after receiving land from the CDA, the PCB had initiated construction of a stadium at Shakarparian. However, the project was abandoned following directions from the Supreme Court. This time, the CDA itself is undertaking the construction of the cricket stadium. Published in Dawn, November 16th, 2026

items.title: CORPORATE WINDOW: Nvidia CEO’s ‘fall from grace’
items.description: It took Jensen Huang more than three decades to build Nvidia into one of the world’s most valuable companies. In just five trading sessions, its shares reportedly plunged 18 per cent, wiping approximately $913 billion off its market valuation. The circumstances surrounding that decline present an extraordinary case study in corporate reputation, institutional power and the consequences of concentrating a company’s credibility in a single individual. Huang, Nvidia’s co-founder and longtime CEO, has publicly acknowledged an extramarital relationship following reports that the woman involved, Chinese business executive Alice Huang, was suspected by American intelligence officials of acting on behalf of Beijing. More recently, allegations of a second relationship, this time involving a senior Nvidia executive reporting directly to Huang, have surfaced, raising further questions about conflicts of interest and leadership accountability. According to a report by The New York Times, US intelligence officials believed Alice Huang may have been recruited by Chinese intelligence. China has rejected the allegations as groundless. There is no established public finding that she engaged in espionage, that Jensen Huang knowingly assisted a foreign intelligence operation, or that sensitive information was compromised. The Nvidia board has initiated an independent investigation. Huang has since resigned. An investigation, of course, is not a verdict. But the reputational consequences of uncertainty rarely wait for one. Huang’s extraordinary influence over Nvidia is inseparable from its success. His long-term conviction about parallel computing helped transform a graphics-chip manufacturer into a company central to the global AI economy. His vision, personal credibility and leadership became powerful corporate assets. Yet therein lies the paradox. The individual who builds an institution can also become its greatest vulnerability. When a company’s identity is inseparable from its founder, personal conduct acquires institutional consequences. Questions surrounding one individual’s judgment can rapidly become questions about an organisation’s governance, integrity and future. The reputational risk is amplified because stakeholders struggle to distinguish between the credibility of the person and that of the enterprise. Reputation has tangible economic consequences, influencing investor confidence, access to capital, commercial relationships, regulatory scrutiny and talent retention. The stakes become considerably higher when the organisation itself is strategically important to a country. Nvidia sits in a unique place defined by artificial intelligence leadership, semiconductor geopolitics, US-China competition and American national-security policy. Huang has played a visible role in discussions between Washington and Beijing over access to advanced computing technology. This raises a broader question about the relationship between private enterprise and national reputation. In an increasingly interconnected global economy, certain corporations have become extensions of their countries’ technological credibility and economic influence. Their commercial decisions can shape diplomatic relationships, trade negotiations and perceptions of national competitiveness. When leadership credibility is questioned, the consequences can, therefore, extend beyond shareholders to governments, international partners and national interests. The challenge is to manage legitimate security concerns without allowing unproven allegations to become judgments about entire countries or communities. For Pakistan, the Nvidia controversy offers a particularly relevant reflection. Across our business landscape, from established family enterprises to emerging technology startups, organisations are frequently built around powerful personalities. Founders become synonymous with their companies, their personal networks drive commercial relationships and their visibility becomes central to institutional identity. This concentration is often deliberate. In environments where institutional trust can be difficult to establish, a credible, charismatic founder can attract investment, open doors and lend legitimacy to a business. But the danger emerges when the founder’s reputation becomes the company’s reputation, when relationships belong to individuals rather than institutions, and when decision-making authority and stakeholder confidence are concentrated in one person. The vulnerability is not necessarily misconduct but dependence. And this is where corporate governance and strategic communications must work together. Pakistani businesses often invest in developing the visibility of their founders and CEOs. Far fewer appear to give comparable attention to the deliberate disbursement of visibility across C-suite leadership, developing multiple credible voices capable of representing the organisation’s expertise, values and strategic direction. This is about more than distributing media appearances. A visible, empowered leadership team signals institutional depth, continuity and the existence of expertise beyond one individual. It reassures stakeholders that the organisation’s future is not entirely dependent on the judgment, relationships or reputation of its founder. But visibility without authority is cosmetic. The distribution of public credibility must be accompanied by genuine delegation of responsibility, independent board oversight and credible succession planning. For Pakistani startups seeking international investment, these considerations are particularly significant. Investors are backing an enterprise’s future, not merely the persuasive abilities or personal networks of its founder. The same principle applies to family-controlled businesses seeking to build institutions that endure across generations. Huang’s leadership helped create extraordinary value. The present controversy does not erase those achievements. But it exposes the fragility that can arise when an institution becomes so closely identified with one person that uncertainty surrounding the individual unsettles confidence in the whole. The question for business leaders is whether they are building organisations that can stand independently of them, or organisations whose fortunes remain inseparable from their own. The ultimate price of concentrated power is revealed when an institution must prove that it can be trusted independently of the person who made it successful. The writer is a strategic communications adviser. Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, November 16th, 2026

items.title: Energy: Crude reality — Is oil glut imminent?
items.description: Oil markets are undergoing a massive shift in sentiment. The Republicans’ thrashing in the mid-term elections, the consequent cooling off the Middle East war theatre, softening global demand, and growing talk of a global surplus have altered crude market fundamentals. Oil markets weakened this weekend. This was a second straight weekly drop in prices. Markets took further cue when US President Donald Trump told reporters that the war with Iran was “effectively over.” Oil prices fell to their lowest level since late August. Both Brent and WTI were down by about 2.5pc last week, after falling by 16pc and 13pc, respectively, the week before that ended Nov 6. On Friday (Nov 13), Brent Crude (January delivery) settled at $95.84 per barrel, while the WTI Crude (December delivery) settled at $88.56 per barrel. After touching $126/barrel in April and talks since then about the possibility of a severe oil shortage due to the blockade of Hormuz, this is a major drop. New fundamentals are taking over oil markets. The world’s oil supply is swinging back to a surplus for the first time since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran, the International Energy Agency (IEA) reported on Thursday last. Falling oil prices offer Pakistan a breather. Various global research reports are unanimous about oil surplus as ME war theatre cools off Oil supplies outstripped demand by almost 2 million barrels per day (bpd) in October, the Paris-based agency said, as “Gulf exports recovered much faster than global oil demand.” The IEA said it expected global oil supply to average 105m bpd in the final three months of the year, 1.7m bpd higher than the demand forecast. The IEA had earlier projected a deficit in Q4 this year. The market was “showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran,” the IEA report added. To ease the supply pressures further, the IEA report said, its members would speed up the release of remaining emergency oil stockpiles pledged earlier this year, adding a further 71m barrels to the market by the end of February 2027. The stocks are held in refineries, oil terminals, power stations and at offshore fields in the North Sea. OPEC+, which also includes non-OPEC oil giant Russia, seems to concur with the IEA report. It reported a substantial surge in its oil production for October 2026, driven largely by Saudi Arabia and Iraq as supplies rebound toward pre-war levels. As per the report, the combined OPEC+ production rose by 2.04m bpd in October to average 41.23m bpd. This volume was almost 97pc of pre-war February levels, while the total OPEC crude production climbed by about 1.96m bpd to reach 27.16m bpd. Saudi output increased by 1.18m bpd to 10.56m bpd, essentially the pre-war production level. Aided by alternative pipelines and workarounds despite ongoing shipping friction, the oil Kingdom has been able to overcome major obstacles, and Aramco’s chief executive is now saying the company plans to raise this further by the year end. Meanwhile, Iraqi output has also increased by roughly 496,000 bpd to 4.49m bpd or higher, marking multi-year highs. The OPEC report citing secondary sources also added that Russian oil production rose by 41,000 bpd in October from September to 8.668m bpd. Using workarounds such as so-called dark crossings through the Strait of Hormuz, where tankers switch off tracking signals to evade attack from Iran, it is being reported now that exports from the region are almost touching the pre-war levels. Investment Bank JP Morgan is also hinting that the growing output is balancing the markets rapidly. “We estimate the global oil market returned to a surplus of 1.1m bpd in September, widening to 1.4m bpd in October, nearly matching last year’s average of 1.3m bpd,” the bank said. Goldman Sachs also estimates the global liquids market was broadly balanced in the September-October period, in contrast to the deficit in March. A marginal surplus from last year, an uptick in production outside of the Gulf, along with a decline in demand, has helped balance the market, the bank said. The recovery in global oil supplies has also eased pressure on emergency stockpiles, which have been diminished by the Iran conflict, the Guardian commented. “It’s clear the biggest fear a few months ago was a fear of shortage,” Reuters reported, citing Phil Flynn, senior analyst with the Price Futures Group. “Now it looks like the biggest fear is a surplus.” In the meantime, demand growth concerns are also taking some shine off the crude oil markets. While OPEC is keeping its global oil demand growth projections unchanged, expecting an increase of 180,000 bpd for 2026 and 2.55m bpd for 2027, averaging 108.3m bpd, the OECD energy watchdog IEA is projecting a fall in global oil demand by 2.68m bpd this year to 103.2m bpd. Consumption is forecast to rebound next year but is still expected to remain below the 2025 levels, with growth mostly in petrochemical feedstocks as the market for vehicle fuel is hit by “high prices, electrification and fuel efficiency,” the IEA report said. The US Energy Information Administration (EIA), the statistical arm of the Department of Energy in Washington, also highlighted in its November short-term energy outlook (STEO) that demand “has fallen considerably during the prolonged oil supply disruption.” “The reduction in oil consumption, particularly in China, has limited the impact the loss of supply has had on global oil prices,” the EIA said. “We now estimate that global liquid fuels consumption will fall by 2m barrels per day in 2026,” it added. “In addition to lower consumption in China, we estimate oil consumption in the Middle East has fallen largely because of reduced air travel and less economic activity,” it continued. But geopolitical risks and resulting threats to the oil markets have not disappeared. Ominous clouds persist. Despite increasing exports from the Middle East, attacks against vessels carrying crude oil, among others, through the Hormuz, the key waterway for crude exports from the main Middle East producers, persist. On Thursday, Iran’s military said four oil tankers were hit by explosions in the waterway after ignoring warnings. Reuters could not immediately verify the Iranian accounts. In Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, the Yemeni Houthis also continue with their attacks. The latest targets included a pumping station on the East-West pipeline, a facility in the port city of Yanbu and an Aramco building in Riyadh. Signals remain mixed. Risk of serious war escalation in the oil-rich region has gone down, yes, but attacks on tankers in the Hormuz persist, while the chances of a peace deal dimmed after President Donald Trump said, “We don’t need a deal with Iran” and that “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” What does all this mean for Pakistan? Prices have gone down, and it will help the country manage its balance of payments better. After all, oil remains the largest drain on its accounts. And though the chances are remote, what if the war theatre reignites? Islamabad has a vested interest in keeping the temperature as low as possible. That should continue! Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, November 16th, 2026

items.title: Cane growers, mills and govt in a fix
items.description: Every year, as November approaches, Pakistan’s sugar sector gets embroiled in a familiar cycle of controversy, uncertainty and competing interests. Growers want millers to start crushing on time, offer fair prices and ensure timely payments. Millers, on their part, cite unsold inventories, uncertainty over export and financial constraints as reasons for delaying operations. Caught between the two, the government struggles to protect consumers by keeping sugar prices affordable without undermining the financial viability of the industry. More often than not, it fails to satisfy either side, leaving the sector mired in uncertainty at the start of another crushing season. This recurring confrontation is more than a seasonal disagreement between farmers and industrialists. It rather reflects the failure of successive governments to evolve a coherent, long-term framework for managing sugarcane production, procurement, processing and marketing. Consequently, what should be a routine agricultural and industrial activity has instead become an annual flashpoint, holding everyone – rural livelihoods, the sugar supply chain and consumers – hostage for the next entire year. In recent years, alongside this annual controversy, an equally contentious pattern has emerged: a recurring cycle of sugar exports, subsequent price hikes and eventual imports. Under pressure from millers, the government invariably allows export, sometimes even subsidising it – ostensibly to earn foreign exchange, offload surplus inventories and help start crushing season. However, as domestic supplies tighten and prices begin to soar, the government scrambles to import sugar to stabilise the market. Farmers are protesting delay in crushing; millers want export of sugar, holding crushing season hostage; the government appears reluctant and the situation is approaching a boiling point. A policy can only be sustainable if it balances the interests of all three parties. Right now, the situation is exactly the same. Farmers are protesting the delay in crushing operations. Millers, not satisfied with export permission of 200,000 tonnes, want to send out another 1.1 million tonnes. The government, bitten by the last experience of export, is reluctant. According to the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics, Pakistan exported approximately 765,734 tonnes of sugar (against permitted 700,000 tonnes) during the first 11 months of FY2024-25, generating around $411 million. These exports were authorised in phases after the government and industry apparently sat together many times and identified a substantial domestic surplus. However, the domestic price situation belied surplus claims. In December 2024, ex-mill sugar price was around Rs125-130 per kg. By June 2025, retail prices jumped to Rs200 per kgi n most parts of the country, and the government approved an import plan for 500,000 tonnes to boost domestic supplies. The SBP in a 2024-25 report linked export with squeezed domestic availability and sugar price trends. It also noted that sugar contributed significantly to urban food inflation during the same period. This reversal raised a fundamental question: how did a country, with surplus stocks for exports, find itself in short supply within months and was forced to import the same commodity? Though the government never answered this question, the critics, however, did. To them, most of the millers belong to, what they pejoratively call, sugar mafia, and the ruling elite and it is the most convenient way to make a windfall of hundreds of billions of rupees within a few months. The State Bank of Pakistan, in its 2024-25 report, linked export with squeezed domestic availability and sugar price trends in the second half of the financial year. It also noted that sugar contributed significantly to urban food inflation during the same period. The foreign exchange argument proved equally false. The average export value during the process was around $537 per tonne. By comparison, the average import price was $575 per tonne. Price differential is a routine when transactions take place at different times, but the comparison does raise questions about the assumptions and consequences of exporting sugar and then importing at a higher price. A briefing to the National Assembly in October 2026 further deflated the export case when it was told that 306,737 tonnes of sugar was imported at a total cost of Rs54.16bn. Approximately 198,668 tonnes had been sold at an average price of Rs168 per kg, while 108,069 tonnes is still with the Trading Corporation of Pakistan, and the government is considering the export option. Now consider the final reality: Pakistan first exported sugar, subsequently imported to restore domestic supplies, and then faced the cost of unsold imported stocks. The ECC this September noted inaccurate demand-and-supply projections and the cost of holding imported sugar stocks. It is not to say that sugar exports or imports are undesirable: both can be justified under appropriate circumstances. The problem is when such decisions are made without reliable assessments of production, consumption, carryover and strategic reserves – or, as critics allege, at the behest of vested interests, the consequences are then borne by all, by consumers through price volatility, by farmers through market uncertainty, and by taxpayers through the costs of inventory management. Millers are once again pressing for export of sugar, with the crushing season being held hostage. The government appears reluctant and the situation is approaching a boiling point. What Pakistan needs, therefore, is not another round of ad hoc and unsubstantiated decisions on exports, imports or prices, but a predictable, long-term, transparent and rules-based policy framework that brings certainty to the sector. To achieve this, it must establish a credible system for assessing sugarcane production, expected sugar recovery, domestic consumption, carryover stocks and exportable surpluses before authorising any exports. It must be linked to independently verified estimates and the maintenance of strategic reserves, rather than granted permission for export under pressure from the industry, later lick price wounds and scramble to contain price increases through import. Similarly, any decision to import sugar should be based on transparent assessments of actual domestic requirements, with clear accountability for procurement costs, pricing and inventory management. Equally important is the need to address the underlying conflict between growers and millers. Crushing should begin at a predictable schedule, growers should receive a fair and timely price, and millers discouraged from using delayed operations as leverage in negotiations over exports. The government must also ensure that its decisions do not disproportionately favour one stakeholder at the expense of others. A policy can only be sustainable if it balances the interests of farmers, millers and consumers. Ultimately, sugar is too important to be managed through annual bargaining, myopic political calculations and reactive interventions. The recurring cycle of surplus claims, export permissions, domestic price hikes and emergency imports reflects a failure on all fronts: policy, planning and institutional coordination. Unless this cycle is broken through credible data, predictable rules and accountability, Pakistan will continue exporting sugar when it believes it has too much, import it when it feels left with too little, and pass the burden on to consumers and taxpayers. Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, November 16th, 2026

items.title: Nigeria: One-party or one-man state? By Suleiman A. Suleiman
items.description: Since at least late 2024, when President Bola Ahmed Tinubu had been in office for barely 18 months, politicians and other Nigerians have been saying that the country is drifting into a one-party state. These warnings have not only grown louder in recent months; they are justified. The All Progressives Congress (APC) now controls 31 out of 36 states, since at least the middle of this year, when the 2027 election campaigns entered top gear. At the end of the 2023 election cycle, the APC controlled 21 states, including the off-cycle election in Edo State in 2024. This means that, in the last year, 10 sitting governors have defected from their original parties to join Tinubu in the APC. The reverse traffic, meanwhile, is zero. This is unlike the 2015 election cycle, when leading politicians were defecting from the then ruling People’s Democratic Party (PDP) to the then main opposition APC. At the same time, the transformation of political organisation and opposition parties that we witnessed during 2013–2015 does not appear to be happening this time, as the leading opposition parties remain ridden by crippling crises that President Tinubu and the APC have been accused of instigating. First of all, the PDP is now a one-man show, and it is difficult to even know what the party stands for or who its leading members are, other than FCT Minister Nyesom Wike. More significantly, in 2023, the Labour Party (LP) and the New Nigeria Peoples Party (NNPP) won 63 seats between them—almost all of them for the first time in history—in the National Assembly elections, and a total of 12 states and the FCT in the presidential election by their candidates, Mr Peter Obi and Dr Rabiu Kwankwaso, combined. That was a formidable performance, particularly by Peter Obi, but both the LP and the NNPP are no longer serious contenders in this election, and the two men have since left to meet on the same presidential ticket in the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC). Accusing fingers also point to Tinubu for making their own political parties unviable platforms for the two men. This leaves the African Democratic Congress (ADC), which faces the most crisis of all. For almost a year, the ADC, formed by a partial coalition of like-minded and opposition interests, has been held hostage by the antics of one man, enabled almost entirely by Nigerian courts. The status of ADC candidates, from the presidential to the state assembly elections, currently hangs in limbo because Nigerian courts in this era now think that the dubious concerns of one party member are more important than the will of all the voters in the hundreds of primary elections conducted by the APC in the past months. In short, Nigeria today looks like a one-party state, with the ruling APC as the last man standing. In my view, however, Nigeria is not sliding into a one-party state. It is already a one-man state. A one-party state—a country where a single political party dominates the political space—is a form of authoritarian rule, whether codified in law or in practical effect. In practice, however, there can be significant checks, political pressure and opposition within the ruling one party itself. More importantly, while undemocratic, one-party states tend to be developmental. They typically maintain political legitimacy through rapid industrialisation and all-round national development, as illustrated by the former Communist countries in Europe, including the defunct USSR, and most strikingly by today’s Chinese Communist Party (CCP), which lifted more than 600 million people out of acute poverty in under 30 years. Tinubu’s APC is nothing like a one-party state in this sense because the twin scaffolds of legitimacy—a serious national development agenda and internal checks—are wholly lacking. Instead, we have a president who straddles his party and the nation without any effective guardrails to his power. That is not a one-party state; it is, rather, a one-man state, whereby nearly all formal institutions of the state, all political parties, civil society, and other informal power brokers no longer provide any meaningful constraints on the will of the president. That is not good for Nigeria, and I am not sure it is something good for the President himself. Since 1999, Nigeria has never really had a true multi-party or two-party system, with the exception of the two-year period between 2013 and 2015. What we have always had is a pseudo-one-party state, whereby a single political party dominates the political space: first the PDP, from 1999 to 2013, and then the APC, during 2015–2023. But even during those years of pseudo-democracy, there were at least two important guardrails against presidential power that ensured that our democracy continued to grow and thrive. First, ruling party politics in Nigeria since 1999 was always characterised by significant political pressure and opposition within the party itself, even in the near absence of an effectively coordinated or strong opposition party. That pressure and opposition came from various factions of the ruling party, or from other centres of power within the party and government. Secondly, there was significant and effective opposition from outside the party and government, particularly from the media, labour unions and organised civil society. The result was that no president was able to win or get everything he wanted all the time. For example, former President Olusegun Obasanjo was the most powerful of Nigerian leaders from 1999 to 2023. But even at the peak of his power, Obasanjo still faced serious pressure and opposition from ruling party chairs, governors, members and leaders of the National Assembly, etc., many of whom frequently disagreed or clashed openly with him. Industrial strikes by unions were effective enough to compel the government to backtrack on some of its policies. Newspapers and civil society organisations were firm and stringent in their criticisms of presidential overreach. It was only natural, then, that Obasanjo’s third-term bid was defeated. Presidents Umar Yar’Adua, Goodluck Jonathan and Muhammadu Buhari were all more or less the same, as significant power blocks within and outside the ruling party and government provided significant checks on their power. The Governors’ Forum was a powerful wedge on Yar’Adua, and, since 1999, the National Assembly was probably most assertive under Buhari’s first term. Governors Uzo Kalu of Abia and Attahiru Bafarawa of Sokoto fought tooth and nail against Obasanjo, not to mention Senate President Chuba Okadigbo, Speaker Ghali Na’Abba and even Dimeji Bankole, just as Governor Ortom screamed at Buhari daily for eight years. If for nothing else, these pressures were useful for defeating Obasanjo’s “third term”, for getting Yar’Adua to initiate enduring reforms in our electoral system, for the doctrine of necessity that made Jonathan President, for forcing Jonathan to accept defeat in the 2015 elections, and for making a democrat out of Buhari—all of which, and more, are important moments of progress in our democratic journey. But my broader point is that all of these guardrails of our developing democracy have been blown off, bought up or buried under the rubble of President Tinubu’s silent corrosion of Nigerian politics, economy and society, leaving us with something worse than a pseudo-one-party state: that is, a one-man state. The ruling APC itself, the National Assembly, the governors, including those pretending to belong to other parties, the courts, the anti-corruption agencies, large sections of the religious and traditional establishment, and equally large sections of the media and so-called “civil society” all appear to be answering to or doing the bidding of one man in Nigeria today. Only Nigerians and their date with INEC in January and February are now left standing. We will see. This article was previously published 11 months ago, but has been updated to reflect current events. The post Nigeria: One-party or one-man state? By Suleiman A. Suleiman appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: PenCom opens up on N52,000 minimum pension guarantee
items.description: By Victor Ahiuma-Young The National Pension Commission, PenCom, has shed light on the implementation of the long-awaited Minimum Pension Guarantee, MPG, disclosing that 173,209 Nigerian retirees are eligible to benefit from a guaranteed minimum monthly pension of N52,500 following its formal activation by President Bola Tinubu. The initiative, aimed at improving the welfare and financial security of retirees under the Contributory Pension Scheme, CPS, was unveiled alongside a healthcare programme designed to provide free access to essential medical services for low-income pensioners. The two initiatives, the Minimum Pension Guarantee and the Pension Industry Healthcare Plan (PenCare), were announced at the Presidential Pension Security Initiatives ceremony held at the State House Banquet Hall, Abuja. Tinubu, who was represented at the event by Senate President Godswill Akpabio, said the Minimum Pension Guarantee fulfilled a provision of the Pension Reform Act 2004, which was retained in the 2014 legislation but had remained unimplemented for 22 years. Declaring the scheme operational, the President assured pension contributors that the government would no longer allow eligible retirees to receive pensions below the guaranteed minimum threshold. “From this day, there is a floor beneath the Nigerian retiree. No one who contributed under the Contributory Pension Scheme will ever be allowed to fall below,” he said. The President urged successive administrations to sustain the policy and periodically increase the guaranteed amount rather than discontinue it. On the healthcare component, President Tinubu said the Pension Industry Healthcare Plan, PenCare, was designed to shield vulnerable retirees from medical expenses that could deplete their retirement savings. He said beneficiaries would receive healthcare access cards in the coming months, enabling them to access essential medical services without bearing the financial burden. The President also disclosed that his administration had issued a N758 billion bond to address outstanding pension arrears and approved a N32,000 monthly consequential adjustment for affected federal pensioners. He added that state governments had collectively spent more than N1 trillion settling outstanding pension obligationsSpeaking at the ceremony, PenCom Director-General, Omolola Oloworaran, disclosed that 173,209 retirees had qualified for the N52,500 monthly minimum pension. She explained that the beneficiaries comprised 34 per cent of retirees from federal service, 12 per cent from state employment and 54 per cent from the private sector. According to her, the guaranteed amount was determined through actuarial validation and would be reviewed periodically to ensure its sustainability. Oloworaran further disclosed that “more than N400 billion is s available in the Pension Protection Fund to support the implementation of the initiative.” She noted that over 65 per cent of private-sector retirees currently received monthly pensions below the newly established threshold, underscoring the importance of the intervention. Providing further details, Oloworaran said the pension industry had committed “more than N7 billion to the programme, with insurance premiums already paid to provide healthcare coverage for nearly 30,000 retirees.” Meanwhile, Chairman of Heirs Holdings, Mr Tony Elumelu, described the initiatives as investments in human dignity, pledging private-sector support for efforts aimed at strengthening retirement security and promoting financial inclusion. Speaking at the event, Elumelu particularly praised the pension industry for funding PenCare, calling it “a powerful demonstration of what responsible institutions can achieve when they put people first.” He assured that “the private sector stands ready to support policies and partnerships that strengthen our institutions.” Framing the programmes within his “Africapitalism” philosophy, which holds that economic growth must “translate into improved lives”, Elumelu added: “I congratulate Mr. President, the leadership of PenCom led by Omolara Oloworaran, and all stakeholders who have made today’s milestone possible.” The post PenCom opens up on N52,000 minimum pension guarantee appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Asean summit opens under cloud of US-China rivalry
items.description: • US president to attend summit and hold first Quad meeting with India, Japan and Australia of his second term • Metro Manila deploys nearly 20,000 police ahead of planned anti-Trump protests • Group unable to conclude negotiations on long-delayed South China Sea code of conduct MANILA: A key regional summit opened in Manila over the weekend, with Southeast Asian heads of state facing questions on trade, security and an ongoing energy crisis while playing host to a who’s who of global leaders. US President Donald Trump is scheduled to arrive on Tuesday near the summit’s conclusion, a visit expected to include a sideline meeting with fellow Quad countries India, Japan and Australia — the first of his second term. The meeting of the Quad — a grouping broadly aimed at counterbalancing China’s regional influence — would come days before a historic sit-down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will sign a new defence pact with host country the Philippines. Nearly 20,000 police officers have been deployed around Metro Manila for the summit, with progressive groups predicting a turnout of thousands on Tuesday for an anti-Trump march on the summit site. Much of the uproar targets the US Pax Silica programme — a supply-chain initiative designed to counter China’s dominance in semiconductors and rare earths — whose flagship Philippine project, a 1,620-hectare AI manufacturing hub north of Manila, threatens to displace Indigenous families. A day of early meetings kicked off on Saturday with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announcing a Philippine trade deal. But two issues that have vexed Asean leaders for years — a languishing South China Sea “Code of Conduct” and their relationship with war-torn Myanmar — look to be Singapore’s problem when the bloc’s rotating chair passes to the city-state in 2027. Asean and China were unable to conclude negotiations on a long-delayed South China Sea code of conduct under the Philippines’ chairmanship, despite reaching provisional agreement on about 80pc of the draft, Manila’s foreign minister said on Sunday. Negotiations on an Asean-China Code of Conduct in the South China Sea have dragged on for over two decades, but the Philippines, as current chair, had committed to speed up those talks and conclude the code this year. “There is no conclusion yet,” Philippine foreign minister Ma. Theresa Lazaro told a press conferenceat a summit of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations in Manila, adding that several key issues remain unresolved, including questions over whether the code would be legally binding. “The Asean countries plus China have also different views on how things are,” she added. China’s Southeast Asian neighbours want the code to be grounded in international law, which they have repeatedly accused Beijing of disregarding as it asserts its sovereignty over nearly all of the South China Sea. Beijing maintains that its actions in the South China Sea have been lawful and professional. Hopes of achieving a so-called Code of Conduct in the disputed South China Sea between Asean states and China during Manila’s year in the chair, meanwhile, have flagged. A Southeast Asian diplomat involved in summit preparations said he did not expect a code to be signed at the summit. Published in Dawn, November 16th, 2026

items.title: Tinubu, 2027 and the price of losing trusted journalism
items.description: By SEGUN ADEDIRAN In London last week, Sarah Lester, editor of the Manchester Evening News, stood before Parliament to open this year’s Journalism Matters campaign. She was not pleading for sympathy. She was asking a question that every democracy must now answer. The British prime minister had promised that “trusted local journalism remains at the heart of communities.” Lester wanted to know what that promise actually meant. How far, she asked, is power willing to go to ensure that journalism does not merely survive, but thrives? It was a British speech, delivered to a British audience, about a British crisis. Yet in the Nigerian media industry, it landed with an uncomfortable familiarity. For Nigeria is facing the same question, only more urgently, and with far higher stakes. We are heading toward 2027. Another general election is approaching. And the institutions that are supposed to make that election legible — the newspapers, the local radio stations, the investigative newsrooms that have held Nigerian democracy together since 1999 — are bleeding out. President Bola Ahmed Tinubu knows this world intimately. He is not a stranger to the press. He is a media proprietor. He was a central figure in the pro-democracy struggle of the 1990s, when independent newspapers were not a luxury but a weapon — printed in secret, distributed at great risk, read as acts of defiance against military rule. He understands, perhaps better than any president before him, that without a free press, there is no democratic contest. There is only noise. In March, when he met with media leaders, the president spoke well. He acknowledged the plight of the press. He promised support. Those words mattered. But promises do not pay for newsprint. They do not keep a bureau in Sokoto open. They do not stop a young reporter from leaving journalism for public relations because journalism can no longer pay rent. That is the question now before the Villa: What will this administration actually do? The crisis is not abstract. It is arithmetic. Hyperinflation has made newsprint, ink, plates and broadcast equipment prohibitively expensive. The naira’s devaluation has turned what was once a difficult business into an impossible one. Advertising, once the lifeblood of newspapers, has migrated to platforms that did not create the journalism they profit from. Google and Meta extract enormous value from Nigerian reporting — our investigations, our headlines, our photographs — while returning almost nothing to the newsrooms that produced them. At the same time, the information environment has become toxic. WhatsApp, TikTok and Facebook are flooded with doctored videos, invented endorsements and AI-generated falsehoods. In an election year, that flood becomes a weapon. When professional newsrooms shrink, misinformation does not merely fill the vacuum. It becomes the vacuum. This is not a sentimental argument for nostalgia. It is a structural argument for democracy. Elections require a shared factual basis. Voters need to know what candidates promised, what governments delivered, what budgets contained, what courts decided. Without trusted local journalism, there is no reliable record. Without a reliable record, accountability collapses. And where accountability collapses, corruption and violence flourish. The world is no longer debating whether to act. It is acting. On Nov. 11, the European Commission formally presented its proposed Digital Fairness Act, aimed at manipulative “dark patterns,” addictive design features like autoplay and infinite scroll, and deceptive influencer marketing. Violators could face fines of up to 6 per cent of global turnover. It recognises that platforms cannot be left to regulate themselves. In Britain, the Competition and Markets Authority has opened an investigation into Meta over new content terms that would allow the company to use publisher content to train its artificial intelligence systems — without fair compensation. The question is no longer whether AI will be built on journalism. It is whether journalism will be paid for it. In the United States, after Democrats swept both chambers in the midterms, incoming lawmakers have signalled hearings with tech chief executives and federal AI oversight legislation. Even President Donald Trump, long resistant to regulation, has said he is open to working with Democrats on AI guardrails — provided they do not cause American innovation to fall behind China’s. And in Africa, the stakes are becoming visible in stark relief. On Nov. 11, after a 248-day suspension, Gabon restored access to Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube — but under new ordinances regulating AI-generated content, requiring personal identification, and establishing direct moderation agreements between the state regulator and the platforms. It is a blunt, imperfect model, but it reflects a continental realisation: unregulated platforms are a threat to sovereignty itself. Nigeria cannot afford to watch this global reordering from the sidelines. Supporting journalism does not mean subsidising sycophancy. It does not mean creating a state press. It means treating independent news as what it is: public-interest infrastructure, as essential as roads and courts. The challenges of elections and campaigns can be daunting. But the President will etch his name in media history if he’s able to fix this digital anomie in record time. A press that is starved into dependence is no more free than a press that is censored into silence. There is a particular irony here. President Tinubu rose to power through a political movement that depended on a fearless press to survive. The newspapers that carried the June 12 struggle, that exposed military excesses, that kept the idea of democracy alive when democracy was illegal — those papers did not survive because they were profitable. They survived because Nigerians believed journalism was worth dying for. Today, journalism is not asking Nigerians to die for it. It is asking the state to stop letting it die of neglect. As we approach 2027, the choice is stark. We can enter the election with a weakened, impoverished press, overwhelmed by AI-generated propaganda and platform-driven misinformation — an election where no one trusts anything, and therefore no one trusts the result. Or we can enter it with a renewed, financially viable, independent press capable of informing voters, checking power and telling the Nigerian story truthfully. Lester warned Britain not to take journalism for granted “even for a second.” Nigeria has taken it for granted for far too long. President Tinubu has a historic opportunity — not merely to praise the press, as he did in March, but to save it. That would be his most enduring democratic legacy. Not a road, not a refinery, but a republic where truth still has a home. The time to act is not after 2027. It is now, before the light dims further. •Adediran is the Chief Executive Officer of the Newspaper Proprietors’ Association of Nigeria The post Tinubu, 2027 and the price of losing trusted journalism appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Awesome
items.description: In Jules Verne’s wildest imagination, the technology that would send humanity starward was already familiar on Earth. The launching mechanism for the American rocket, in Verne’s 1865 novel From the Earth to the Moon , is—of all things—a colossal cannon. The speed required to reach the lunar surface, he reasoned, would require a gunshot of a launch. So in Vernian terms, a starship was not merely launched but “fired” into space. I’ve been thinking of Verne today as I watched the video (then watched it again, and again) of SpaceX’s latest history-making maneuver. Yesterday, for the first time ever, engineers successfully pulled off a midair landing —using the company’s Mechazilla tower’s “chopstick” arms to snatch a starship the size of a skyscraper out of the sky after it had spent the past 22 hours in Earth’s orbit. Up until this point, Mechazilla’s chopsticks had caught boosters after launch—that is, the part of the rocket that detaches—but never ships themselves. You really do have to watch the video for yourself, and when you do, try to remember this: Starship 42—the largest and most powerful rocket in the world—just successfully launched, went into orbit, took 14 victory laps around the Earth at some 17,000 miles per hour, deploying more than two dozen Starlink satellites as it went, before careening into our atmosphere then swiveling upright so it could glide gently into a pair of robot arms waiting below. Every aspect of what took place is unbelievably hard to achieve, but let’s begin with the absolute violence of reentry. A rocket in orbit goes fast, so fast it is difficult to visualize, something like 20 times faster than the speed of sound, and certainly faster than a bullet (or, for that matter, a cannonball). When the starship approaches the Earth’s atmosphere, traveling five miles a second, several things happen in quick succession: Engineers fire a single engine against the direction of travel, in order to steer it back toward Earth belly-first. This move is less about slowing the ship down—it barely does—and more about achieving the right orientation so that the heat shield coating the belly of the starship can double as, essentially, a giant brake against the air of the atmosphere. Only the thinnest traces of air wisp through space, and therefore a rocket in orbit encounters no heat-producing friction. But as the ship suddenly collides with the air of the atmosphere, an enormous shock wave forms. Friction with the atmosphere heats up the air around the ship until it turns into superhot plasma, which envelopes the starship in a terrifying-gorgeous orange glow. (The glow makes a bit more sense when you realize that the plasma approaches 13,000 degrees Fahrenheit, hotter than the surface of the sun.) From there, the ship is still falling Earthward horizontally, and slowing down as it does so. Yesterday, a crowd assembled in Texas to see if SpaceX could actually land it. They first heard a sonic boom—people cheered at the sound—shortly before Starship 42 appeared, a black obelisk belly-flopping its way through the clouds. What happened next was the flip maneuver that resembled, as SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell put it , “alien-level technology.” When the ship was less than one mile from the ground, it had to go from falling flat to falling in an upright position, so that the chopstick arms of the tower below could catch it. To do this, engineers re-lit the ship’s engines and used sophisticated steering mechanisms to swing the ship vertical. Seconds later—roughly 21 seconds by my count—the rocket floated down to the two long arms of the tower with improbable elegance. “It was almost magic,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman posted on X after the successful landing. And it really was. It is not an exaggeration to say that almost no one believed this was possible. Even SpaceX’s most devoted engineers had their doubts. The aerospace engineer Tom Mueller, whom Musk hired as SpaceX’s first employee in 2002, recently appeared on a podcast where he described the meeting, several years ago, where Musk first presented the idea of plucking a rocket out of midair as it landed. The idea was, “ We’re going to catch it in the air on chopsticks, like catching a fly with chopsticks ,” Mueller recalled, “and we all just rolled our eyes like This is crazy. There’s just no way. ” He went on: “Some of us did not believe it could be done.” They were wrong, and beautifully so. (Musk, who five years ago teased the idea of the chopstick landing by tweeting a GIF of Mr. Miyagi, reported yesterday that he hugged Starship 42 upon its return.) The lesson for Mueller—and this was something he said even before yesterday’s triumph—was this: “It’s not hype. He’s going to build it. I believe if it’s possible, it will be solved. And it might take longer than Elon thinks, but he will solve it.” (I should note here that it is possible to acknowledge two things at once: that Musk is an omnidirectional boor, and also that he builds awesome rockets.) Our species has never struggled to dream up the impossible. But humans are often ambivalent, and cynical, when technological change inevitably arrives. This is understandable. Life is so short, and most tech revolutions and their consequences span generations. Even the most dedicated historians simply don’t have the time or perspective to see clearly and completely what it means for humanity when our most daring technological ideas are realized. Long before Verne, Cyrano de Bergerac invented his own fictional rocket—also powered by gunpowder—in his posthumously published 1657 novel, The Other World . But it is Americans who tend to see the impossible as a kind of dare. Uncommon audacity is, to paraphrase Verne, an American birthright. (Although Musk is South African by birth, he is American by choice.) Verne’s writing was laced with satire about the national character, a fact that is sometimes ignored today. More recently Verne is remembered mostly for his prescience—Neil Armstrong always delighted in the fact that Verne’s space voyagers eventually splashed down in the Pacific Ocean, just as he did when he returned from the moon. But it’s worth lingering on the cynicism underlying Verne’s satirical views today. Where Italians had their music and Germans had their philosophy, Verne wrote in From the Earth to the Moon , Americans had their guns. The novel was premised on the idea that, when the Civil War ended, Americans would mourn the end of fighting because they didn’t have a reason to focus their ingenuity on the making of ever-more-powerful weaponry. And so, on that “sad and melancholy” day that peace arrived following a war that killed hundreds of thousands of Americans, a small group of them decided to pivot from guns to the moon—a dream that would enable them to engineer the impossible with a “Platonic kind of artillery.” (Verne’s work was prescient not just on a technical level, it turned out: He also anticipated the commercialization of science.) In Verne’s imagination, Americans went to the moon not because they dared to do the impossible, but because they wanted to fire a cosmically powerful weapon. In reality, when Americans reached the moon, they left behind a stainless-steel plaque bearing the following inscription: Here men from the planet Earth first set foot upon the Moon, July 1969 A.D. We came in peace for all mankind. Back home on Earth, people sometimes lament those among us who can’t help but gaze skyward. Why go to space , they ask, when there is so much work to be done here on this planet? I’d like to say this attitude is understandable, but the truth is that I’ve always seen it as reflecting a false binary, one that imposes limits on what we can achieve and one that assumes there is nothing more to be gained from a tremendous technological achievement than the achievement itself. One of the tricks that technology plays on us is that it sometimes leaves the impression of permanence—that a machine or system that works fairly well, or even extraordinarily well, in a certain way, is proof of an end state. But every technological system that becomes obsolete does so because it is replaced with a wholly new way of understanding the world and humanity’s place in it. We learned that sound waves can be recorded and played back, that electricity can be harnessed, that cathode rays allow us see through solid matter, that chemists can cure epidemics of childhood death, that the telephone is portable, that the telephone is in fact a computer , that you can lift up a glass rectangle and use it to see someone—and talk to them in real time!—through the glowing portal of its screen, and that the machines themselves can talk. This is not to say that every technological change is inherently good for humanity, because of course it is not. The resilience of our species, our impressive adaptability in the face of constant change, is one of our superpowers. It is also the quality that numbs us to the impositions of new technology that we ought to reject. However, human resilience cuts the other way, too. It can dull our sense of wonder about what is possible when humanity attempts to do something that almost no one believes can be done. This weekend, SpaceX achieved the impossible. Tomorrow, someone else will, too.

items.title: États-Unis : plus de 19.000 vols annulés après une panne liée au remplacement de câbles vétustes
items.description: Le trafic aérien américain a été fortement perturbé ce week-end après une panne survenue dans les infrastructures de contrôle aérien. À l’origine de cet incident rarissime : le remplacement d’anciennes lignes de communication en cuivre par de la fibre optique, qui a entraîné une défaillance en cascade et provoqué plus de 19.000 annulations de vols. Les autorités américaines espèrent un retour progressif à la normale d’ici dimanche soir. La panne avait notamment conduit à la suspension de tous les décollages aux États-Unis pendant plus de quatre heures vendredi après-midi. Selon les données communiquées par l’autorité américaine de l’aviation civile, quelque 12.000 vols ont été annulés vendredi. Samedi, plus de 6.400 annulations avaient déjà été recensées parmi les 41.000 vols programmés. Plus de 1.000 autres annulations étaient encore enregistrées dimanche matin. L’incident serait lié à une opération visant à remplacer des câbles en cuivre vieillissants par de la fibre optique sur des infrastructures utilisées par le contrôle aérien. Selon le ministre américain des Transports, Sean Duffy, un routeur est tombé en panne à la suite de ces travaux, provoquant des perturbations dans les communications avec les avions ainsi que dans certains systèmes radar. Le patron de la Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Bryan Bedford, a expliqué que l’instabilité s’était progressivement propagée dans le système. Face aux risques potentiels, les autorités ont décidé de suspendre temporairement les décollages à travers le pays. Une mesure exceptionnelle, déjà prise en 2023 à la suite d’une panne informatique et, avant cela, après les attentats du 11 septembre 2001. Des milliers de passagers bloqués dans les aéroports La panne a rapidement provoqué une importante désorganisation dans les principaux aéroports américains. Files d’attente, vols annulés à répétition et voyageurs contraints de passer la nuit dans les terminaux ont marqué le week-end. À l’aéroport LaGuardia de New York, plusieurs passagers ont raconté avoir subi plusieurs changements de vols avant de finalement se retrouver bloqués jusqu’au début de la semaine suivante. La situation a également affecté les équipages et les appareils, compliquant la reprise progressive du trafic. Même après le rétablissement du système, les perturbations doivent donc se poursuivre le temps que les compagnies réorganisent leurs programmes. Washington veut accélérer la modernisation Cet incident intervient alors que la vétusté des infrastructures du contrôle aérien américain fait depuis longtemps l’objet de critiques. Le calendrier est d’autant plus sensible que la Maison Blanche a demandé aux parlementaires, à la veille de la panne, d’approuver une enveloppe supplémentaire de 30,1 milliards de dollars destinée à moderniser le système. Sean Duffy a estimé que les besoins pourraient même atteindre 50 milliards de dollars, plaidant pour la mise en place d’un système entièrement modernisé afin de limiter les risques de nouvelles défaillances. La panne a toutefois déclenché une polémique politique à Washington. Plusieurs élus démocrates reprochent à l’administration Trump de ne pas avoir engagé suffisamment tôt les investissements nécessaires dans les infrastructures aériennes. La gouverneure démocrate de l’État de New York, Kathy Hochul, est même allée jusqu’à réclamer la démission du ministre des Transports, dénonçant les défaillances répétées du système aérien américain. Alors que les autorités espèrent une normalisation du trafic d’ici dimanche soir, les conséquences de cette panne pourraient encore se faire sentir dans les prochains jours, le temps de résorber les retards accumulés et de repositionner les équipages et les appareils. The post États-Unis : plus de 19.000 vols annulés après une panne liée au remplacement de câbles vétustes appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: OIF: la Francophonie comme une cocotte-minute!
items.description: «Réinvestir dans la paix pour une prospérité partagée et une stabilité durable». C’est le thème qui porte le 20e sommet de l’Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF), qui est accueillie par Phnom Penh. Pourtant, de mémoire de francophone, c’est bien la première fois que la paix et la stabilité sont autant menacées au sein de cette institution qui peine, depuis quelques années, à rayonner sur le monde, tant sur les plans politique, économique que diplomatique. Pourtant, à sa création en 1970, ses pères fondateurs, notamment le Nigérien Hamani Diori, le Sénégalais Léopold Sédar Senghor, le Cambodgien Norodom Sihanouk, ou le Tunisien Habib Bourguiba, lui avaient juste donné pour mission, la promotion de la langue française, de la diversité culturelle et linguistique, de la paix, de la démocratie et les droits de l’homme, tout en appuyant l’éducation et la recherche, et à booster la coopération. Mais se qui préoccupe aujourd’hui une OIF qui a perdu en 2025, des membres et non des moindres, comme le Burkina Faso, le Niger et le Mali, c’est la désignation de son secrétaire général, entre trois Africaines et un Européen. A la suite du retrait de la candidate de la République démocratique du Congo (RDC), Juliana Lumumba, la Mauritanienne Coumba Bâ et la Rwandaise Louise Mushikiwabo, qui compte briguer un troisième mandat, seront, ce lundi 16 novembre, dans la capitale cambodgienne, les challengers du Roumain Dacian Ciolos. Et c’est là que tout se complique pour l’OIF qui attend une désignation sous haute tension, voire, pour la première fois dans l’histoire de l’institution, une élection crisogène. A l’accoutumée, le, ou la, Secrétaire général de l’OIF est le fruit d’un consensus. Un rituel que le président français Emmanuel Macron s’échine, en vain, à faire prospérer, au profit de son candidat, l’ancien Premier ministre Dacian Ciolos. En tout cas, le Rwanda qui refuse toute imposition du choix du président français Emmanuel Macron, est prêt à aller jusqu’au vote, tout comme la Mauritanie qui s’oppose également à tout retrait de sa candidate. Si le proverbe dit que «la nuit porte conseil», celle qui aura précédé la désignation, ce lundi, du SG de l’OIF, même en absence de toute réunion formelle sera certainement riche en tractations, en compromis, et même en compromissions. Avant l’annonce tant attendue de l’identité du ou de la SG, toutes les cartes seront proposées, battues et rebattues, car les enjeux de la désignation ont d’ores et déjà pris le pas sur ceux de l’Organisation qui se cherche entre crise du multilatéralisme et les tensions internes qui la mine. Au titre de ces frictions, vient en pôle position, celle entre le Rwanda et la RDC, les Congolais accusant leur voisin de soutenir activement les combattants de l’AFC-M23, mouvement politico-militaire, désormais avalé par le Front pour la Refondation de la Nation (FRN), dirigé par l’ancien président Joseph Kabila. Du reste, si la Rwandaise Louise Mushikiwabo est reconduite à la tête de l’OIF, la RDC pourrait claquer la porte de l’Organisation! Ainsi donc, la «guerre» entre le Rwanda, par FRN interposé, et la RDC, s’est déportée dans la capitale cambodgienne et constitue, désormais, une menace de plus pour une OIF qui a du mal à supporter son gigantisme en effectif et un budget bien fragilisé qui porte difficilement ses ambitions. Que, il ou elle arrive par consensus ou par vote, le secrétaire général de l’OIF aura bien du mal à recoller les morceaux d’une institution qui, assurément, perdra beaucoup de plumes au cours de ce 20e sommet. Pour la Francophonie, il y aura, certainement, un avant et un après Phnom Penh! Par Wakat Séra L’article OIF: la Francophonie comme une cocotte-minute! est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Development challenges in Delta: Ebitonmo’s theory of political thermodynamics
items.description: By Enewaridideke Ekanpou Alapala Anthony Ebitonmo, the man currently representing Burutu North Constituency in the Delta State House of Assembly, is again furious, as it is his wont to be, resistant to every benevolent arrester unleashed on him. Rather retrospectively, in a blazing fury, he was recently sighted at Oyangbene and approvingly led into the open arms of people carrying “chalked hearts.” The hearts of Oyangbene people became immediately “chalked” because Ebitonmo was suddenly sighted. Even in their variedly chalked hearts at the sight of the man, they were confounded, thrown off balance, when they were told he had not come for Oyangbene community. Even in their confoundment, they sought to know the rationale behind Ebitonmo’s sudden appearance in Oyangbene when he claimed openly he had not come for the Oyangbene community. In a characteristic blazing fury, he was curtly categorical that his sudden appearance was rooted in two propellants—Serikoromo Primary School and his famed theory named political thermodynamics. Available statistics reveal Serikoromo Primary School in Burutu Local Government Area of Delta State had been the home of rickety structures for decades, daily rendezvoused by pythons, leopards, elephants, lions, grasscutters, lizards, iguanas, rats, cats, and bats. To teachers and pupils, these reptiles and mammals became the bandits troubling them. For decades, they cried their eyes out with tears that spread like the waters of the Atlantic Ocean. However, their impassioned tears looked like the silvery waters in the ocean; they were not comforted like the weeping Biblical Martha. Serikoromo Primary School, founded in 1956, was where I had my primary education in 1988. The oceanic tears of this school had known many decades of neglect. Awakened to the pathetic story of Serikoromo Primary School, Ebitonmo became blazingly furious. With a blazing fury that carried the troubling pains of the poor teachers and pupils, Ebitonmo risked a sudden flight to Serikoromo Primary School without a visible speedboat professionally skimming the white waters of Oyangbene River. His presence in the school was equivalent to ritualistically stepping on “Atu” in a folktale stunningly told by TimiebiMaika. Mystically, as captured in Timiebi’s folktales, ritualistically stepping on the “Atu” was imbued with the power to make one appear dramatically at the backyard of one’s house. The power of invisibility and disappearance dwells mystically in the “Atu” ritual. The second propellant of Ebitonmo’s appearance in Oyangbene without a visible flight was his treasured philosophy of political thermodynamics. Political thermodynamics is the measurable degree of responsiveness of, or applicability of, core developmental ideas to visible development challenges that plague communities and mankind in general. It is the space for the transformation of strategically formulated developmental ideas into enduring visible structures through the interrogative interaction between formulated developmental ideas and the real challenges of development that trouble mankind in different dimensions of life. It is a pragmatic interrogative interface aimed at the delivery of visible, measurable structures of development. Political thermodynamics also centres on creating a measurable merger between electoral promises and visible structures—visible structures viewed as emanations from the electoral promises upon which the representational mandate of Ebitonmo stands. Ebitonmo thinks endlessly in development terms for both biotic and abiotic factors in Burutu North Constituency. For Ebitonmo, Serikoromo Primary School was another experimentation ground for a measurable test of his theory of political thermodynamics underlying all his political and representational conversations, interactions, and engagements as a singular ideational propelling force. At work, political thermodynamics shows how Ebitonmo’s ideational formulations flow and confront core development challenges of the people, transforming them in pragmatic terms into visible and measurable structures, in demonstration of the dominance of his developmental formulations over visible development challenges. In Ebitonmo, the merger between theoretical formulations and pragmatic delivery is demonstrably visible. This is what Ebitonmo has just demonstrated at Serikoromo Primary School in Oyangbene. Ebitonmo’s journey to Oyangbene is driven by his blazing fury that my primary school is abandoned, and this abandonment has consumed many years. He is also driven by his political thermodynamics theory, or his prized philosophy of representation. This theory centres on how his humanistic political ideas interact with core development challenges of the people at the grassroots level. His humanistic ideals merge into the developmental challenges of the people to transform lives measured in infrastructure. His ideas confront the development problems, solve them, and transform the people. His theory is a measure of how humanistic ideas transform lives through interaction with and confrontation of their core developmental problems. Every community touched by him is a reflection of how his philosophy of political thermodynamics bulldozes and transforms communities through visible projects executed. In every move, Ebitonmo is guided by his famed political thermodynamics philosophy—a political philosophy his political opponents cannot match strength for strength and idea for idea. Pragmatic and indestructible, political thermodynamics is inspiring and striking in its theoretical composition and applicability. Though an inspiring and striking political theory it is, it must be admitted that thermodynamics, from which Ebitonmo’s political thermodynamics is derived, was foundationally erected and came into being through the scientific exertions of multiple scientists in the 19th century, like Rudolf Clausius, James Watt, William Thomson (Lord Kelvin), Walter Nernst, and others. However, among the multiple scientific exertions which gave birth to thermodynamics, Nicolas Leonard Sadi Carnot was widely acclaimed as the father of thermodynamics based on his successful publication on thermodynamics in 1824. The decades-old governmental neglect of Serikoromo Primary School has just been ended by Ebitonmo through his phenomenal display of blazing fury on flight to Oyangbene without a visible flight. In Serikoromo Primary School, an architecturally arresting block of four classrooms now bestrides the compound like an angelic creature on a visit of no return to the school. Pride has been restored to the school where I had my primary education. I can now proudly “pound” my chest and proclaim ubiquitously that I was the senior prefect of Serikoromo Primary School in 1988. No special sermon or discourse is further required to attest to the viability of Ebitonmo’s theoretical formulations encapsulated in his philosophy of political thermodynamics. Either for a visible block of classrooms or visible desks and tables for teachers and pupils, Ebitonmo’s developmentally audacious philosophy of political thermodynamics has been felt in Okpokunou, Edegbene, Enekorogha, Bikorogha, Gbekebor, Obotebe, Ayakoromo, Gbekebor, Kiagbodo, Opuapale, Labolouseigha, and Bubougbene in Burutu North Constituency. Representationally building a verifiable merger between theoretical formulations and pragmatic delivery is not an easy task, but Ebitonmo has just achieved it without a flourish. This is commendable in every dimension. To pull off this representational feat, representational encore is the natural harvest, the stipend, the appreciatory recognition of this performance. The political thermodynamics theory of Ebitonmo is too viable and relevant to be ignored by this generation. The scaffolding needed for this viable political philosophy to thrive must be afforded a space. This means the people of Burutu Constituency must speak the unifying language of “bitter kola” in the 2027 general elections. The language of bitter kola spoken in the waiting 2027 general elections, we are sure of Ebitonmo’s developmentally blazing fury and his beloved philosophy of political thermodynamics, whose pragmatic power of developmental communication has been asserted in Serikoromo Primary School. Historically, Ebitonmo has become the fearless arrester of dilapidated structures in Serikoromo Primary School, Oyangbene. A referentially bold and furious arrester Ebitonmo has become, steadily reinforced and sustained in every step by Governor Sheriff Oborevwori’s MORE agenda. *Dr. Ekanpou writes from Akparenogbene, Delta State. The post Development challenges in Delta: Ebitonmo’s theory of political thermodynamics appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: DPRK slams Japan's proposed exception to Three Non-Nuclear Principles
items.description: The Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) on Sunday condemned Japan's consideration of an "exception" allowing the introduction of nuclear weapons in emergencies in its security documents to be revised this year, calling it a prelude to the realization of Japan's nuclear ambition. A commentary published by the Korean Central News Agency said Japan's "dangerous neo-militarist moves" aimed at disrupting the postwar international order and changing the regional balance of power were "running toward the realization of its nuclear ambition." The official news agency described the move as a dangerous scheme to turn Japan into a military giant "with the help of US nukes" and "lay a springboard for its own possession" of nuclear weapons. The commentary said criticism of the current Japanese government's neo-militarist moves was growing at home, while regional and international communities were also "strongly denouncing and opposing" its attempts to revise its nuclear policy. It described the proposal as "nothing but a cunning trick" to conceal Japan's intentions, quell criticism at home and abroad, and gradually dismantle the restrictions under the "Three Non-Nuclear Principles."
